Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the deeper layer, reporting that Ibn Jarīr transmitted this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Wahb through several chains of narrators. Having consulted her government and gained their confidence, she developed a strategy: to test out Sulayman's real intention. She needed to know which of two men she was dealing with:

- **If he was only a king** wishing to expand his empire by subjugating her kingdom, then his motives were worldly, the gift would satisfy him, and a different plan would be needed to face the challenge.
- **If he was truly a prophet** conveying the message of Allah, then he would agree to nothing other than acceptance of Islam — and in that case his command should be followed and no hostility adopted against him.

Ibn Kathir preserves the same test in the queen's own blunt words, from Ibn ʿAbbās and others: "If he accepts the gift, he is a king, so fight him; but if he does not accept it, he is a Prophet, so follow him."

This is why the gift is not merely a bribe — it is an instrument of investigation. She is spending treasure to buy information about a man's soul.

Qatādah's comment on her, quoted by Ibn Kathir, is full of warmth: "May Allah have mercy on her and be pleased with her — how wise she was as a Muslim and (before that) as an idolator! She understood how gift-giving has a good effect on people." It is a rare and generous thing: an early scholar praying for a queen who, at the moment described in this ayah, had not yet believed.

**A note on the fuller story.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays, from Qurṭubī, a long account of the envoys' arrival — a floor of gold and silver bricks laid out for thirty miles, four thousand chairs of gold on either side of the hall, the envoys embarrassed by the gold bricks they had brought when they saw animals standing on gold, and Sulayman finally returning all their gifts and answering all the questions Bilqīs had sent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself introduces this material as "Historical Isra'ili legends." It is worth knowing as background colour, but it is not the Qurʼān's own account, and nothing in your faith should rest on it. What the Qurʼān chose to record is not the décor of the throne room but the words Sulayman spoke.

## "Do you offer me wealth?" (ayah 36)

Ibn Kathir says that more than one of the scholars of tafsīr among the Salaf and others stated that she sent him a huge gift of gold, jewels, pearls and other things. And then this detail, which is the heart of the passage: it is apparent that Sulayman, peace be upon him, **did not even look at what they brought at all** and did not pay any attention to it. He turned away, and rebuked them.

Three sentences, each doing different work:

**أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمَالٍ** — rendered "Will you help me in wealth?" and, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "Are you giving me an aid of wealth?" Ibn Kathir catches the sting: *are you trying to flatter me with wealth so that I will leave you alone with your Shirk and your kingdom?* They have misjudged him at the most basic level.

**فَمَا آتَانِيَ اللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا آتَاكُمْ** — "What Allah has given me is better than that which He has given you." Ibn Kathir explains: what Allah has given him of power, wealth and troops is better than that which they have. Note that even in the moment of refusing, Sulayman does not say *what I have is better*; he says *what Allah has given me*. The credit runs straight back to the Giver.

**بَلْ أَنْتُمْ بِهَدِيَّتِكُمْ تَفْرَحُونَ** — "Nay, you rejoice in your gift!" Ibn Kathir's reading: *you are the ones who are influenced by gifts and presents; we will accept nothing from you except Islam or the sword.* The rebuke is diagnostic. Their delight in the treasure reveals what they actually value, and it exposes why they assumed it would work on him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders his answer to the envoys directly: whatever wealth and bounties Allah has given me is much better than your wealth and material — therefore I do not accept your presents of wealth; you better take them away and enjoy them yourselves.

## Is it allowed to accept gifts from non-Muslims?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the fiqh question that ayah 36 obviously provokes, since Sulayman's refusal might be read as a general prohibition. Its answer is that the ruling turns on consequence:

- If accepting would **lead to weakening of one's own position or that of the Muslim community**, or is likely to go against the community's genuine interests, then it is prudent not to accept. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī here.)
- If **the interest of the Muslims favours acceptance** — for instance if the gesture may lead the non-Muslim towards accepting Islam, or may ward off some impending danger — then it is permitted.

The evidence offered is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ himself, who accepted presents from some and rejected them from others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from ʿUmdatul Qārī Sharḥ al-Bukhārī (Kitāb ul-Hibah) and Sharḥ as-Siyar al-Kabīr, on the authority of Kaʿb ibn Mālik, that ʿĀmir ibn Mālik — the brother of Barāʾ — went to Madinah on some work while he was still a disbeliever and presented two horses and two pairs of garments to the Prophet ﷺ, and he sent them back with the remark that presents are not accepted from disbelievers. Likewise, when ʿIyāḍ ibn Ḥimār al-Mujāshiʿī presented him something, the Prophet ﷺ asked whether he was a Muslim; when he said no, the gift was returned, with the explanation that Allah had commanded him not to accept presents from the disbelievers. Against these stand other narrations reporting that he ﷺ **did** accept: a piece of leather from Abū Sufyān while he was still a disbeliever, and a very shiny piece of fine silk from a Christian.

Shamsul Aʼimmah, cited in ʿUmdatul Qārī, comments after these narrations that in his view the reason for the difference was this: where the Prophet ﷺ judged that **rejecting** would bring the disbeliever near to Islam, he rejected; where he considered that **accepting** would help bring him close to Islam, he accepted. The measure throughout is the person's guidance.

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the discussion with the point that ties it back to the story: Bilqīs took the rejection of her presents as a sign of prophethood — not because accepting gifts from disbelievers is impermissible, but because *she had purposefully sent hers as a bribe*, in order to save herself from any attack. A man who cannot be bought is not chasing a kingdom.

## "Go back to them" (ayah 37)

The final ayah is the message the envoys carry home. Ibn Kathir notes that "Go back to them" means *with their gift* — the caravan returns loaded exactly as it came, which is itself half the message.

Then: "We verily shall come to them with armies that they cannot resist" — Ibn Kathir: they have no power to match them or resist them — "and we shall drive them out from there in disgrace," meaning driven out in disgrace from their land, "and they will be abased," meaning humiliated and expelled.

Read this against ayah 34 and the passage turns full circle. The queen had said that kings ruin a town and make the most honourable of its people the lowest; now she hears something like the very outcome she feared named back at her. But the cause is not the same. Sulayman is not coming to plunder a city and enrich himself — he refused the wealth. The terms he offers are the terms of a prophet.

And the outcome, as Ibn Kathir relates it, is that the test worked. When her messengers came back to her with her undelivered gift and told her what Sulayman had said, she and her people paid heed and obeyed. She came to him with her troops in submission and humility, honouring Sulayman and intending to follow him in Islam. And when Sulayman, peace be upon him, realised that they were coming to him, he rejoiced greatly — the joy of a prophet is over a soul turning to Allah, not over a caravan of gold.

## What the passage asks of us

**Decide with counsel.** If the Prophet ﷺ, who had revelation, was still commanded *and consult them in the matter*, then no one else has a case for deciding alone. And the queen's technique is worth copying: tell people sincerely that their view matters before you ask for it, and you will get their honesty and their loyalty together.

**Follow the evidence, even against your interest.** She had a council willing to fight and every worldly reason to defend her throne. Instead she designed a test, committed in advance to following his command if the answer came back "prophet," and then — hardest of all — she kept her word.

**Know what you cannot be bought with.** Sulayman's greatness in ayah 36 is not that he had more gold; it is that he did not look at theirs. He measured what was offered against **what Allah has given me** and found the offer beneath consideration. Every one of us is offered something to look away from the truth — money, standing, an easier life. The question the passage puts to us is the one the envoys were made to feel: *are you the sort of person who rejoices in the gift?*

passages.title: The throne, the glass palace, and her submission
passages.tafsir:
This is the closing scene of the story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) and Queen Bilqis. She is on the road to his court, and before she arrives he arranges two encounters that strip away everything she has trusted in — her throne, and her own eyes. The thread running through ayat 38–44 is one question: **when a person comes face to face with something greater than themselves, what will they do with it?** Sulayman answers it in ayah 40 with gratitude; she answers it in ayah 44 with submission.

## Where she is when ayah 38 begins

Ibn Kathir relays from Muhammad bin Ishaq, from Yazid bin Ruman, what happened when her envoys came home. She said: "By Allah, I knew he was more than a king, and that we have no power to match him, and that we can gain nothing by being stubborn with him." So she sent word ahead — "I am coming to you with the leaders of my people to see what you will instruct us to do and what you are calling us to of your religion". Her throne, gold inlaid with rubies, chrysolite and pearls, was to be placed in the innermost of seven rooms, one within the other, every door locked. She told her deputy: let no one approach it or even see it until I return.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds, on Qurtubi's authority, that her envoys came back "dumb-founded and awe-struck", and that she told her people plainly that he was no ordinary king but was on a special assignment from Allah, and that fighting His messenger is like fighting Allah Himself.

One caution: Maʿārif ul Qurʾān notes in a footnote that **no authentic record is available for these details**; they come from Israelite traditions, and the figure of twelve thousand chiefs each commanding a hundred thousand men is, in the words of ʿAllāmah Ālūsī quoted there, so exaggerated that the report "seems to be a lie." Read such details as colour, not as creed.

Meanwhile Sulayman had sent the jinn to bring him news of her progress and route every day and night. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān records that he saw a cloud of dust in the distance and asked what it was, and was told, "O messenger of Allah! Queen Bilqis is coming with her people" — by some narrations she was then about three miles from his court. That is the instant of ayah 38.

## "Before they come to me submissively" — one word worth pausing on

Sulayman says: *qabla an yaʾtūnī muslimīn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān stops here, because **muslimīn** carries two layers. Its plain lexical meaning is *obedient, submissive*; in conventional usage "Muslim" is the equivalent of "believer". Ibn ʿAbbās held it is the literal meaning here, precisely because at that moment it was not established that she had accepted faith. Her belief comes later, after she speaks with Sulayman. So ayah 38 describes a queen coming in submission, not yet in faith; everything Sulayman arranges next is meant to move her from the first to the second.

That is why Maʿārif ul Qurʾān says he decided she should witness, beyond royal grandeur, **a prophetic miracle** — one that should help her convert to faith. Why the throne in particular? Presumably because it was the most secured object of her treasure, kept under lock in the innermost of the seven halls, where even her own people could not reach; to shift something so huge and so secured, so far, without breaking a lock or a door could not have been possible without the help and will of Allah. It was, as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān puts it (citing Ibn Jarīr), the ideal way to make her realise both the unlimited power and control of Allah and that Sulayman's high position and status was **bestowed** on him by Allah.

## The two volunteers: strength and knowledge

Ayah 39 gives the first offer. An **ʿifrīt** of the jinn speaks up — Mujāhid glosses ʿifrīt as "a giant jinn"; Abū Ṣāliḥ said "it was as if he was a mountain." His pledge: *before you rise from your place* — Ibn ʿAbbās explains, "before you get up from where you are sitting," and As-Suddī and others note that Sulayman used to sit to pass judgements and rulings over the people, and to eat, from the beginning of the day until noon. So the ʿifrīt is offering a few hours. Then he adds his credentials: *innī ʿalayhi la-qawiyyun amīn* — **strong and trustworthy**. Ibn ʿAbbās unpacks both words exactly: strong enough to carry it, and trustworthy with the jewels it contains. A complete offer — capability plus integrity. And it was not enough: Ibn Kathir reports that Sulayman replied, "I want it faster than that."

Ayah 40 gives the second offer. The speaker is described not by his power but by what he carries: *alladhī ʿindahu ʿilmun mina l-kitāb* — "the one with whom was knowledge of the Scripture." His pledge is *before your glance returns to you*: Ibn Kathir explains it as, lift your gaze and look as far as you can, and before you get tired and blink, you will find it before you. The jinn measured his speed against a morning; the man of knowledge measured his against a blink.

According to Ibn Kathir: **he got up, performed ablution, and prayed to Allah**, may He be exalted. Mujāhid says his words were, "O Owner of majesty and honour." No exertion, no display, only wuḍūʾ (ablution) and duʿāʾ (supplication). Strength reached for the throne; knowledge reached for Allah.

## Who was he? Where the scholars differ

The Qurʾān does not name him, and the commentators divide.

- **One view: it was Sulayman himself**, because his knowledge of the Book of Allah was the most extensive. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān raises this possibility; on that reading the event is a *muʿjizah*, a prophetic miracle, the objective being that she should experience it so that no doubt was left in her mind.
- **The other view: it was one of his companions.** Ibn Jarīr reports this from many commentators including Qatādah, and Qurtubi declares it the position of the majority. Ibn ʿAbbās said, "This was Āṣif, the scribe of Sulayman." Muhammad bin Ishaq, from Yazid bin Ruman, names him Āṣif bin Barkhiyāʾ, a truthful believer who knew the Greatest Name of Allah. Qatādah said simply, "He was a believer among the humans, and his name was Āṣif." Other narrations in Maʿārif ul Qurʾān say a cousin of Sulayman possessed the knowledge of *al-Ism al-Aʿẓam* — a particular Name of Allah whose speciality is that whatever is invoked from Allah by reciting it is granted.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān reconciles the views: this does not prove Sulayman lacked knowledge of the Greatest Name; rather it is quite likely he considered it prudent for the miracle to be manifested **through one of his people**, since that would leave a deeper impression on Bilqis — which is why he addressed the assembly rather than acting himself.

## Miracle, karāmah — and a view the commentary answers

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān defines terms — crediting the explanation to *Aḥkām ul Qurʾān* by Maulana Ashraf ʿAlī Thanawi rather than offering its own independent verdict.

A **muʿjizah** (miracle) and a **karāmah** (a wonder occurring through someone who is not a prophet) are alike in nature. Both take place without any involvement of natural phenomena — the Qurʾān states the principle in *"You did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw"* (8:17). Crucially, **neither takes place by the wish or control of the person through whom it appears**, but only by the will and act of Allah. The single difference is the recipient: through a prophet it is a miracle, through a non-prophet a karāmah. The commentary adds that unusual acts performed by the righteous are in fact a reflection of the perfections of their prophet, and are in turn deemed miracles of that prophet. So if the speaker was Āṣif bin Barkhiyāʾ, this was his karāmah.

Shaikh Muḥiyyuddīn Ibn al-ʿArabī declared the episode a *taṣarruf* of Āṣif — something like mesmerism or hypnotism, which does not require the one exercising it to be a prophet, a saint, or even a Muslim; since prophets avoid taṣarruf, he explained, Sulayman had Āṣif do it. **The answer given is that the Qurʾān has declared the act the result of *knowledge of the Book*.** In the light of the Qurʾān's own wording, it seems preferable that it was the outcome of some supplication or of the Greatest Name — which falls within karāmah, and has nothing to do with taṣarruf.

One difficulty is handled honestly. The confident "*I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you*" gives the impression of an act carried out with intent and control, which karāmah is not. The answer given: presumably Allah had already given the signal that if there were a desire for it, He would fulfil it in no time. The certainty lay in the promise of Allah, not in the man.

## Ayah 40's second half: the response of a servant

The throne appears. Sulayman does not say *look what I did*. He says: **"This is by the grace of my Lord — to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful."**

First he assigns the blessing to its true owner — Ibn Kathir: "this is one of the blessings which Allah has bestowed upon me." Second, and more startling, he identifies the blessing itself as a **test**. Most of us think of trials as losses; Sulayman sees that the greatest gift he has just witnessed is an examination paper with two answers: shukr (gratitude) or kufr (ingratitude).

Then he draws the conclusion that empties it of self-importance: *"whoever is grateful, truly his gratitude is for himself; and whoever is ungrateful — certainly my Lord is Ghaniyy, Karīm."* Ibn Kathir places this beside *"Whosoever does righteous good deed, it is for himself; and whosoever does evil, it is against himself"* (41:46) and *"whosoever does righteous good deed, then such will prepare a good place for themselves"* (30:44). Your gratitude does not enrich Allah; it furnishes your own house.

The two divine names say why. **Ghaniyy** (Rich) — He has no need of His servants or their worship. **Karīm** (Bountiful) — He is Bountiful in and of Himself, even if no one were to worship Him; His greatness does not depend on anyone. Ibn Kathir pairs this with the words of Mūsā: *"If you disbelieve, you and all on earth together, then verily Allah is Rich, Owner of all praise"* (14:8).

It is recorded in **Sahih Muslim** that Allah, may He be exalted, says: "O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, mankind and jinn alike, were all to be as pious as the most pious among you, that would not add to My dominion in the slightest. O My servants, if the first of you and the last of you, mankind and jinn alike, were all to be as evil as the most evil one among you, that would not detract from My dominion in the slightest. O My servants, these are deeds which I am recording for you, and I will judge you according to them, so whoever finds something good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself."

That is the doctrine of ayah 40 in one breath: nothing we do reaches Him; everything we do reaches us.

## Ayat 41–42: the disguised throne, and a queen who does not guess

*"Disguise her throne for her, that we may see whether she will be guided, or she will be one of those not guided."* Ibn Kathir explains the purpose: Sulayman ordered some of its features altered so that he could test her and see whether she recognised it and how composed she would be. How was it altered? Ibn ʿAbbās: "Remove some of its adornments and parts." Mujāhid: whatever was red made yellow and the reverse, whatever was green made red — everything altered. ʿIkrimah: "They added some things and took some things away." Qatādah: it was turned upside down and back to front, with additions and subtractions. Then in ayah 42 she arrives and is asked, *"Is your throne like this?"*

The object should be far away behind seven locked doors. It looks like hers, and it does not. A lesser mind would leap: *that is my throne* — wrong about the alterations; or *that is not my throne* — wrong about the substance. She says: ***kaʾannahu huwa*** — "as though it were the very same."

Ibn Kathir describes her as wise and steadfast: she did not hasten to say that this was her throne, because it was far away from her; nor to deny it, when she saw that things had been altered and changed. Of her few words he says, **"This is the ultimate in intelligence and strong resolve."** What is praised: an answer reporting exactly as much as the evidence supports and no more — a discipline of speech, and part of what made her ready for guidance.

The rest of ayah 42 — *"and knowledge was bestowed on us before her, and we had submitted to Allah"* — Mujāhid says was spoken by Sulayman.

## Ayah 43: a sentence the scholars read two ways

*Wa ṣaddahā mā kānat taʿbudu min dūni-llāh* — the Arabic parses differently depending on what is taken as the subject of *ṣadda* ("turned away / prevented").

- **Mujāhid and Saʿīd bin Jubayr** (may Allah be pleased with them both) read it as a continuation of Sulayman's speech from ayah 42: what stopped her from worshipping Allah alone was *that which she used to worship besides Allah, for she was of a disbelieving people*. Ibn Kathir says what they said is good; it was also the view of Ibn Jarīr.
- **Ibn Jarīr** noted a further possibility: that the subject of the verb refers to Sulayman, or to Allah.

Ibn Kathir then weighs in: Mujāhid's opinion is supported by the fact that **she declared her Islam only after she entered the ṣarḥ** — so at this point she is still held back by her inherited worship. Note the two forces the ayah names: what she personally worshipped, and the people she came from. Inherited religion is a wall, and it took a prophet and two signs to bring it down.

## Ayah 44: glass, water, and the last illusion

*"Enter the ṣarḥ."* Ibn Kathir explains the vocabulary. **Ṣarḥ** means a palace or any lofty construction — Allah reports Firʿawn saying to his minister Hāmān, *"Build me a ṣarḥ that I may arrive at the ways"* (40:36); the word is also used for the high constructed palaces of Yemen. **Mumarrad** means sturdily constructed and smooth. **Qawārīr** means made of glass, built with smooth surfaces.

What Sulayman had commanded the shayāṭīn to build was a huge palace of glass with **water flowing beneath it** — a layer of glass between a person walking and the water. So when she saw it she thought it was a pool, and uncovered her legs to wade in — until Sulayman told her: *"Verily, it is a ṣarḥ mumarrad of qawārīr."*

The passage's final lesson is aimed at the eye. She was sure enough of what she saw to lift her hem, and she was wrong. She had already learned that a locked fortress means nothing before the power of Allah; now she learns that even her own senses can report confidently and falsely. Ibn Kathir says the palace was built to show her the greatness of Sulayman's authority and power — and that when she saw for herself what Allah had given him and how majestic his position was, she submitted to the command of Allah and acknowledged that he was a noble Prophet.

Her words are the climax of the whole account: ***"My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit, together with Sulayman, to Allah, the Lord of all that exists."***

Ibn Kathir reads each half. *"I have wronged myself"* — by her previous disbelief and shirk, and by the fact that she and her people had worshipped the sun instead of Allah. Notice she does not say *I was misled*; she takes the harm as harm she did to her own soul. *"I submit, together with Sulayman, to Allah"* — following the religion of Sulayman, worshipping Allah alone with no partner or associate, the One who created everything and measured it exactly according to its due measurements.

And notice the name she chooses for Him: **Rabb al-ʿālamīn**, Lord of all that exists. A queen who ruled one kingdom now names the Lord of all of them. That is the true throne of this passage, and it was never hers.

## What the Qurʾān does not tell us

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws a line where the Qurʾān draws one: the story ends with her acceptance of faith; on what happened afterwards the Qurʾān is silent. Asked whether Sulayman married her, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUyaynah answered that her case has finished at *"I submit, together with Sulayman, to Allah, the Lord of the worlds"* — the idea being that where the Qurʾān has not divulged anything further, it is not for us to probe. Ibn ʿAsākir did report, on the authority of ʿIkrimah, that Sulayman married her afterwards, that she was retained as sovereign of her country and sent back to Yemen, that he used to visit her every month for three days, and that he had three palaces built for her there which had no parallel of their kind — and Maʿārif ul Qurʾān closes that report by noting that Allah alone knows best.

## Living it

**Answer like her.** *"As though it were the very same"* — say exactly what you know, and no more. Ibn Kathir called that the ultimate in intelligence and strong resolve.

**Answer like him.** When something wonderful lands in your hands, the first sentence out of your mouth decides everything: *this is by the grace of my Lord* — and the gift is itself the exam.

**Reach for the right instrument.** The mountain-sized jinn was strong and trustworthy and still came second to a man who made wuḍūʾ and called upon Allah.

**Distrust the surface.** She was sure there was water there. Much of faith is the discipline of not letting a first impression become a final verdict — about a floor, about a person, about your own soul.

passages.title: Thamud: Salih, the nine plotters, and empty houses
passages.tafsir:
This passage tells the story of Thamud and their prophet Salih: a single call to worship Allah alone, a nation that splits over it, a mocking demand for punishment, an accusation that the believers themselves are bad luck, and finally a conspiracy of nine men that Allah turns back on their own heads. What holds ayat 45–53 together is one movement — **from a message, to a refusal, to a plot, to empty houses** — and one lesson repeated at every stage: the people who thought they were arranging events were themselves being arranged.

## One sentence of daʿwah, two parties (ayah 45)

Salih is sent to Thamud as **"their brother"**, and his message is compressed into two words: *aʿbudū Allah*, worship Allah. Ibn Kathir sums up the errand exactly so: Allah sent him "to call them to worship Allah alone, with no partner or associate." Everything that follows in the passage is the fallout of that one demand.

Then comes a sudden turn: *fa-idhā hum farīqāni yakhtaṣimūn*, "then look! They became two parties quarrelling with each other." Mujahid explained the two parties simply: **"These were believers and disbelievers."** Ibn Kathir points to the parallel scene in Surah al-Aʿraf, where the arrogant chiefs challenge the weak among them who believed — "Know you that Salih is one sent from his Lord?" — and the believers answer, "We indeed believe in that with which he has been sent," and the arrogant reply, "Verily, we disbelieve in that which you believe in" (7:75–76).

Notice who lines up on which side. In that scene the split is not random: the **weak** believe, the **arrogant** refuse. Truth does not divide a society along lines of intelligence or access — it divides it along the line of pride.

## "Why are you in such a hurry for the bad?" (ayah 46)

Salih's response opens with *yā qawmi* — "O my people." Even here, he is still addressing them as his own.

His question turns on two words: *why do you seek to hasten **the evil** before **the good**?* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unlocks what these refer to. The disbelievers had been demanding that Salih bring the divine torment down on them in this world, so that they might know whether he was truthful. So **"evil" in this sentence stands for the torment**, and **"good" refers to their repentance and their invoking of divine mercy**. The verse then means, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān phrases it: "Why are you asking me to bring the divine punishment before you repent?" Ibn Kathir's reading is the same: *why are you praying for the punishment to come, and not asking Allah for His mercy?*

There is a whole theology of order in that question. Punishment and mercy are both real; the only issue is which one you reach for first. And Salih immediately names the door that is still open: *"Why do you not seek Allah's forgiveness, that you may receive mercy?"*

That single line is worth pausing over. These are people who have already rejected a prophet and demanded that Allah destroy them — and the invitation to *istighfār*, seeking forgiveness, is still extended to them, with mercy attached to it as the hoped-for result. The passage that ends with a nation reduced to rubble contains, in its middle, an open offer of forgiveness that was refused.

## "You are bad luck" (ayah 47)

Their answer is one of the most revealing lines in the surah: *iṭṭayyarnā bika wa-biman maʿak* — "We augur an omen from you and those with you."

Ibn Kathir gives the plain sense of what Thamud meant: **"We do not see any good in your face and the faces of those who are following you."** And he adds the sociology of it: since they were doomed, whenever anything bad happened to any of them, they would say, *"This is because of Salih and his companions."* Mujahid said simply, "They regarded them as bad omens."

Ibn Kathir shows this is a recurring habit of rejecters across the Qur'an, not a one-off:

- Fir'awn's people: when good came to them, "Ours is this," and when evil afflicted them, they saw it as an omen about Musa and those with him (7:131).
- Those addressed in Surah an-Nisa: "If some good reaches them, they say, 'This is from Allah,' but if some evil befalls them, they say, 'This is from you.'" The answer given is decisive: **"Say: All things are from Allah"** (4:78) — meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, by virtue of His will and decree.
- The dwellers of the town who told the messengers, "For us, we see an omen from you; if you cease not, we will surely stone you" — and were answered, "Your omens are with yourselves!" (36:18)

The pattern is always the same: credit ourselves for the good, blame the messenger for the bad. It is a way of never having to examine yourself.

**Salih's reply cuts underneath the accusation entirely.** *Ṭā'irukum ʿinda-Llah* — "Your omen is of Allah." Ibn Kathir explains the force of it: Allah will punish you for that. There is no fortune to be read off a face or a run of misfortune; whatever reaches you comes by Allah's will and decree, and your own record with Him is what you should be worried about.

Then: *bal antum qawmun tuftanūn* — "nay, but you are a people that are being tested." Qatadah said: **"You are being tested to see whether you will obey or disobey."** Ibn Kathir adds that the apparent meaning of *tuftanūn* is: you will be left to get carried away in your state of misguidance. What they were calling bad luck was in fact a trial, and they were failing it while blaming the omens.

## Nine men "who made mischief and would not reform" (ayah 48)

The camera now narrows from a whole nation to nine individuals: *tisʿatu rahṭin* — "nine *raht*."

The word *raht* is used for a group rather than an individual, and the commentators handle this differently. **Ibn Kathir** takes it as meaning simply nine people. **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** suggests each of the nine is called a *raht* presumably because they were regarded as superior among their clan for having wealth and dignity, **each one having his own separate group of people behind him** — hence they are called nine groups. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that they were known as the chiefs of Hijr, the city of the people of Salih, which it describes as a well-known city of Syria. Ibn Kathir makes the same point about their power: **"They forced their opinions on the people of Thamud, because they were the leaders and chiefs."**

Their description is deliberately double-edged: *yufsidūna fi'l-arḍi wa-lā yuṣliḥūn* — "who made mischief in the land, and would not reform." It is not enough to say they did harm; the verse closes the other door too. There was no compensating good in the ledger.

Who were they? Al-ʿAwfi reported that **Ibn ʿAbbas** said: "These were the people who killed the she-camel" — and Ibn Kathir clarifies that the slaughter happened upon their instigation, since Allah says elsewhere, "But they called their comrade and he took a sword and killed the she-camel" (54:29) and "When the most wicked man among them went forth" (91:12). One man's hand did it; nine men's influence drove it. Responsibility does not stop at the person holding the blade.

Ibn Kathir then records something startlingly specific. ʿAbdur-Razzaq said that Yahya bin Rabiʿah As-Sanʿani told them that he heard **ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah** explain "who made mischief in the land" as: **"They used to break silver coins."** They would break off pieces from them — as if, Ibn Kathir notes, they used to trade with them in terms of numbers rather than weight, as the Arabs used to do. And Imam Malik narrated from Yahya bin Saʿid that **Saʿid bin al-Musayyib** said: *"Cutting gold and silver coins is part of spreading corruption on earth."*

Ibn Kathir is careful about how to take this. What is meant, he says, is that the nature of these evil disbelievers was to spread corruption on earth by every means possible, **one** of which was the practice these Imams mentioned. In other words, coin-clipping is not the whole meaning of the ayah; it is one telling example. And what a revealing one — the same men who would soon swear an oath to murder a prophet were also quietly tampering with the money their neighbours traded with. The Qur'an counts that kind of cheating as *fasād fi'l-arḍ*, corruption in the land.

## The oath sworn in Allah's name (ayah 49)

*Taqāsamū bi-Llah* — "Swear one to another **by Allah**." They invoke the name of the very Lord whose messenger they intend to kill. Ibn Kathir: they took a mutual oath, pledging that during the night, whoever met Allah's Prophet Salih, peace be upon him, he would assassinate him. Earlier in the same passage Ibn Kathir describes the shape of the plan: they plotted to let him sleep with his family at night, then assassinate him, and then tell his relatives that they knew nothing of what had happened to him — and that they were telling the truth, because none of them had seen anything.

That cover story is written into the ayah itself: *"then we will surely say to his near relatives: 'We witnessed not the destruction of his household, and verily, we are telling the truth.'"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the ugly cleverness of it. The plan was that all of them together should attack in the darkness of night; then, when the claimant of the blood came forward, they would say that they did not kill him and did not know who had killed him — and in saying so they would have uttered the truth, because no one could have known who had killed whom in the darkness of the night.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes a striking lesson: here were men carrying out infidelity, disbelief, killing and pillage, **and yet they were careful not to speak a lie or be blamed for falsehood**, for the sake of their self-respect. That shows how great the sin of falsehood is, that even the perpetrators of heinous crimes avoid it. If a conspirator's sense of honour recoils at lying, what should a believer's do?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also raises a question the ayah quietly leaves open: the *walī*, the heir, was a man of Salih's own family — so why leave him out of the assassination? Three possibilities are offered: he might have been the successor from the point of view of lineage while himself being an infidel and a party with them; or there could have been the consideration that he might claim compensation for Salih's blood because of his relationship with him; or he might have been a Muslim who enjoyed a prominent position, so that killing him carried the risk of uprising and reprisal among the people. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes with the scholar's honesty: **only Allah knows best.**

## "They plotted a plot, and We planned a plan" (ayah 50)

*Wa-makarū makran wa-makarnā makran wa-hum lā yashʿurūn* — "So, they plotted a plot, and We planned a plan, while they perceived not." They knew about their own plan. They had no idea about Allah's.

Ibn Kathir states the outcome plainly: **"But Allah planned against them and caused their plot to backfire."** Mujahid said: "They took a mutual oath pledging to kill him, but before they could reach him, they and their people were all destroyed."

Ibn Kathir preserves a fuller account, from ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Abi Hatim, of how the plot backfired. After they killed the she-camel, Salih said to them: *"Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. This is a promise that will not be belied"* (11:65). They said: "Salih claims that he will finish with us in three days, but we will finish him and his family before the three days are over."

Salih had a place of worship in a rocky tract in a valley, where he used to pray. So they set out one night to a cave there, saying: "When he comes to pray, we will kill him, then we will return. When we have finished him off, we will go to his family and finish them off too." Then Allah sent down a rock upon them from the mountains round about. They feared that it would crush them, so they ran into the cave — and the rock covered the mouth of the cave while they were inside. Their people did not know where they were or what had happened to them. So Allah punished some of them here and some of them there, and He saved Salih and the people who were with him.

Read that again slowly. The **hiding place they chose** became the tomb. The **ambush position** became the trap. They took shelter from the falling rock in exactly the spot they had picked for murder — running, in fear, into their own grave. That is what *"while they perceived not"* looks like in practice.

## Empty houses (ayat 51–52)

*Fa-nẓur kayfa kāna ʿāqibatu makrihim* — "Then see how was the end of their plot!" The ruin is left standing to be looked at. And the destruction is total: *Verily, We destroyed them and their nation, all together* — the conspirators and the nation whose leaders and chiefs they were.

*Fa-tilka buyūtuhum khāwiyah* — "These are their houses in utter ruin." Ibn Kathir glosses *khāwiyah* with one word: **deserted**. The houses are not really the point; the emptiness is. These were people who had homes and rank in a well-known city, and what remains is silence.

*Bimā ẓalamū* — "for they did wrong." The ruin is not blind fate; it is the just consequence of *ẓulm*, wrongdoing. And then the closing frame: *"Verily, in this is indeed an Ayah for people who know."* Ruins are visible to everyone; the **sign** in them is visible only to those who bring knowledge to what they are looking at.

## "And We saved those who believed" (ayah 53)

The passage does not end in rubble. *Wa-anjayna'lladhīna āmanū wa-kānū yattaqūn* — "And We saved those who believed, and had *taqwā* of Allah," those who were faithful and were mindful of Him.

Two things are named, not one: *īmān*, belief, and *taqwā*, that mindfulness of Allah which the translation of this ayah renders as being "mindful" of Him. These were the believers of ayah 45's split — the party Thamud blamed for every misfortune, the ones told to their faces that no good was seen in them. Ibn Kathir's account ends there too: Allah punished some of them here and some of them there, **and He saved Salih and the people who were with him.** They held no power in Hijr. They were the ones left standing.

## What this asks of us

**Do not read misfortune as omens.** Salih's reply in ayah 47 dismantles the whole business: "Your omen is of Allah." No good or ill fortune is written on a person's face, whatever Thamud claimed to see in Salih's — "all things are from Allah" (4:78), by His will and decree. And blaming one's misfortune on righteous people is, in this passage, the mark of those who refuse to look at themselves.

**Reach for the good before the bad arrives.** Ayah 46 is a standing invitation: seek Allah's forgiveness, that you may receive mercy. The tragedy of Thamud is not that mercy was unavailable — it was offered in the same breath as the warning — but that they wanted a demonstration of the punishment more than they wanted repentance.

**Take the definition of corruption seriously.** These men are condemned in ayah 48 for making mischief and never reforming, and the Imams cited by Ibn Kathir include tampering with the coinage under that heading — though Ibn Kathir is clear that this is one example among every means possible, not the whole meaning. Cheating in what people trade and rely on is not a small private matter; it is filed here under corruption in the land.

**Guard your tongue from falsehood.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's observation on ayah 49 should sting: men planning a prophet's murder still would not let themselves be blamed for a lie. A believer's aversion to lying should run at least that deep, and far deeper.

**Leave the outcome to Allah.** They plotted, and He planned, and they perceived not (ayah 50). For anyone who feels outmatched by people with power, influence and a plan, ayah 53 is the answer the whole passage has been building toward: believe, keep your *taqwā*, and the rescue is Allah's affair, not yours.

passages.title: Lot rebukes his people and is delivered
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat give us the story of Lut (Lot), peace be upon him, compressed into a single exchange: a prophet's question, his people's reply, and what Allah did with each side afterwards. What holds the passage together is that shape — **a rebuke (54–55), an answer (56), a rescue and a ruin (57–58)** — and the fact that the "answer" in ayah 56 is not an argument at all, but a demand to get rid of the man who spoke.

## What Lut was actually warning them about

Ibn Kathir opens his comment plainly: Allah is telling us about **His servant and Messenger Lut**, peace be upon him, and how he warned his people of Allah's punishment "for committing an act of immorality which no human ever committed before them" — intercourse with males instead of females. Ibn Kathir calls it a major sin.

That phrase — *no human ever committed it before them* — is worth sitting with. The Qur'an does not present this as one vice among many that every nation has always had. It presents it as something this particular people brought into the world; and the ayat that follow show them not merely doing it, but moving to expel anyone who objected.

## "While you see" — ayah 54

Lut's rebuke comes as a question: **أَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ وَأَنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ** — *"Do you commit immoral sins while you see?"*

The weight falls on the last phrase, **wa antum tubṣirūn**, literally "while you are seeing". Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *while you see one another, and you practise every kind of evil in your meetings.* That is a devastating detail. Sin that hides is one thing; sin performed in company, in front of each other, in the gatherings where a society does its business, is another. They watched one another do it, and nobody looked away.

A rebuke framed as a question also does something a flat statement cannot. Lut is not informing them of a fact they had missed; he is holding their own conduct up in front of their eyes and asking them to look at it.

## "Nay, you are a people who behave senselessly" — ayah 55

The second question sharpens it: **أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ شَهْوَةً مِنْ دُونِ النِّسَاءِ** — *"Do you practise your lusts on men instead of women?"* — *min dūn an-nisā'*: desire directed at men *to the exclusion of* women.

Then the verdict: **bal antum qawmun tajhalūn** — "Nay, but you are a people who behave senselessly." The verb comes from *jahl*, ignorance. But Ibn Kathir's gloss shows what kind of ignorance is meant: *you do not know anything of what is natural or what is prescribed by Allah.*

Ibn Kathir sets alongside it the parallel passage where Lut says the same thing in other words:

> "Go you in unto the males of mankind, and leave those whom Allah has created for you to be your wives? Nay, you are a trespassing people!" (26:165–166)

Notice the pairing between the two verdicts Ibn Kathir places side by side: here they are *jāhilūn*, people who behave senselessly; there they are *ʿādūn*, a trespassing people — people who cross a limit.

## The only answer they had — ayah 56

**فَمَا كَانَ جَوَابَ قَوْمِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا** — "There was no other answer given by his people except that they said…"

Read the wording carefully: *no other answer… except*. Nothing at all counted as their reply but this. Not a defence, not a counter-argument, not even a denial that they were doing it. Their entire response to a prophet's reasoning was a motion of expulsion:

> "Drive out the family of Lut from your city. Verily, these are men who want to be clean and pure!"

Read that last line again. **إِنَّهُمْ أُنَاسٌ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ** — "they are people who keep themselves pure." It is meant as the *charge against them*. Purity had become the accusation. When a society has gone far enough, the objectionable thing is no longer the sin — it is the person who declines to join in.

Ibn Kathir explains what is going on underneath the sneer: *they feel embarrassed because of the deeds you are doing, and because you approve of your actions, so expel them from among yourselves, for they are not fit to live among you in your city.* The presence of clean people made them uncomfortable, and rather than change, they moved to remove the discomfort. And note the phrase **min qaryatikum** — "from *your* city." In their own mouths, the city was theirs and Lut's household did not belong in it.

Ibn Kathir's closing note on this ayah is the hinge of the whole passage: *So the people resolved to do that, and Allah destroyed them, and a similar end awaits the disbelievers.* They passed their resolution. Allah passed His.

## A note from ayah 49

Our source material also carries the comment of Maarif ul Quran on ayah 49, a few ayat earlier, where the people of Salih (peace be upon him) swear: *"We shall attack him and his family at night, then will say to his heir, We did not witness the destruction of his family and we are really truthful."*

Maarif ul Quran draws out something startling. The plan was to attack in the dark so that afterwards, when the claim for blood was made, they could say they did not know who had killed whom — and in saying so they would have spoken the literal truth, since nobody could have known in the darkness. These men were prepared for murder and pillage, yet they took care not to be caught in a lie. As Maarif ul Quran puts it, this shows how great the sin of falsehood is, that even the perpetrators of heinous crimes avoid it for the sake of their self-respect.

(The same commentary raises a second question — why the plotters left out Salih's heir — and offers more than one possibility: that he might have been an unbeliever aligned with them, or a Muslim of such standing that killing him risked an uprising. It closes with the scholars' proper formula: *Only Allah knows best.*)

## Delivered — and left behind — ayah 57

**فَأَنجَيْنَاهُ وَأَهْلَهُ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ** — "So We saved him and his family, except his wife."

They said *drive them out*; Allah says *We saved him*. The exit they intended as a humiliation was his deliverance.

Then the exception, and it is a painful one. **قَدَّرْنَاهَا مِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ** — "We destined her to be of those who remained behind." Ibn Kathir spells out what "remaining behind" amounted to: *she was one of those who were destroyed, with her people.*

Why? Ibn Kathir gives the reason precisely: *because she was a helper to what they did and she approved of their evil deeds. She told them about the guests of Lut so that they could come to them.* Her crime was collaboration and consent — she gave the city the information it wanted.

Then a remark of Ibn Kathir's that repays slow reading: *She did not do the evil deeds herself, which was because of the honour of Lut and not because of any honour on her part.* Her outward record was clean — but on Ibn Kathir's reading, that outward cleanliness was owed to the dignity of the prophet she was married to, not to anything in her.

Two lessons stand out from this one exception:

- **Approval is participation.** She is destroyed with the doers though she did not do the deeds herself, because she was "a helper to what they did" and "approved of their evil deeds."
- **Closeness to the righteous saves no one by itself.** She shared Lut's house and his name; she did not share his deliverance.

## The rain of those who were warned — ayah 58

**وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ مَّطَرًا** — "And We rained down on them a rain."

The Qur'an leaves the word bare: *a rain*. Ibn Kathir tells us what actually fell: *stones of Sijjil, in a well-arranged manner one after another* — and he adds the description "marked from your Lord; and they are not ever far from the evildoers." Not a chaotic hail, then, but something ordered and deliberate: each stone marked, arriving in sequence.

Then the verdict on the whole episode: **فَسَاءَ مَطَرُ الْمُنذَرِينَ** — "So evil was the rain of those who were warned."

The people are not named here by their sin. They are named **al-mundharīn**, "those who were warned." That is the description chosen for them at the moment of destruction, and Ibn Kathir explains it exactly so: *those against whom proof was established and whom the warning reached, but they went against the Messenger and denied him, and resolved to drive him out from among them.*

Notice how the tafsir closes the circle. The warning had arrived and the proof had been established — and what Ibn Kathir names as their offence at the end is precisely the thing they said in ayah 56: they resolved to drive the Messenger out.

## Living it

The passage is short on commands and long on pattern, so take from it what the sources actually put there:

**Say the true thing, even when you are the only one saying it.** Lut spoke a plain word to an entire city and got a deportation order for it. That was not a failure of his mission; ayah 57 shows how Allah settled it.

**Watch what you approve of, not only what you do.** Ibn Kathir's explanation of Lut's wife is the sharpest line in the passage: she did not commit the act, and it did not save her, because she helped and she approved. In an age when approving is a thing one does with a thumb, this is not an abstract point.

**Take truthfulness as seriously as the plotters of ayah 49 did.** If men bent on murder still guarded their tongues against a lie, the person who prays and fasts can afford no less.

**Do not hear "he thinks he's so pure" as an insult.** In ayah 56 it is the highest compliment in the passage, spoken by people who could not hear what they were saying.

**And do not treat a warning as an insult either.** The people of Lut are described at the end as *al-mundharīn* — the warned. The warning had reached them and the proof had been established; that is how Ibn Kathir explains the word. Every one of us has had the message reach us too.

passages.title: Who creates and sustains? Ask the idolaters
passages.tafsir:
After a long run of prophetic stories — nations warned, nations destroyed — the surah turns and speaks directly to the listener. Ayah 59 tells the Prophet ﷺ to close that section with praise and peace; ayat 60–64 then put a series of questions to the idolaters, each built on the same pattern: *Who does this? Is there any god beside Allah?* The opponents already agree on the evidence; they simply refuse the conclusion.

## Ayah 59: how to end an account of the prophets

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the placement. After recounting the earlier prophets and earlier peoples, and the punishments they faced, the Prophet ﷺ is told to voice gratitude to Allah — for his own followers have been exempted from punishment of that kind in this world — and then to send peace on the earlier prophets and on those mindful of Allah. That is the reading the majority of commentators adopted; some held instead that this sentence is addressed to Lūṭ (peace be upon him).

Ibn Kathir unpacks each half. **"Praise be to Allah"** — praise and thanks for His countless blessings on His servants, and for His exalted attributes and most beautiful names. Praise is owed not only for what Allah gives but for what Allah *is*. **"and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen"** — the ones He selected out from among the rest.

Two readings sit side by side in the sources:

- **The prophets and messengers.** The view of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam and others, supported from the close of Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt, which pairs the same two elements in the same order: *"Glorified be your Lord, the Lord of honour and power, above what they attribute to Him! And peace be on the Messengers! And all praise be to Allah, Lord of all that exists"* (37:180–182).
- **The Companions of Muhammad ﷺ.** This was said by al-Thawrī and al-Suddī, and something similar is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Ibn Kathir sees no conflict: the Companions too were among the servants Allah chose — "although the description is more befitting of the Prophets." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a consequence of Ibn ʿAbbās's reading: if the chosen ones here include the Companions, there is a case for saying *ʿalayhis salām* — "peace be upon him" — over non-prophets as well (a discussion it defers to Sūrah al-Aḥzāb, 33:56).

**A practical ruling from this ayah.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ, draws out the etiquette of any address, sermon or lecture: it should start with the praise of Allah, and then ṣalāh and salām upon the prophets. This had always been the practice of the Prophet ﷺ in his addresses, and his Companions carried it further — beginning not only their addresses but all their important undertakings with praise of Allah followed by ṣalāh and salām upon the Prophet ﷺ.

## "Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?"

The second half of ayah 59 turns to the opponents. Ibn Kathir calls this a question aimed at denouncing the idolaters for worshipping others besides Allah. It is not a genuine comparison but the opening move that forces them to state a position they cannot defend.

## The refrain: *amman… a-ilāhun maʿa'llāh*

Each of ayat 60–64 opens with **amman** — "Or who is it that…" — and each returns to **a-ilāhun maʿa'llāh**, "Is there any god *with* Allah?" Ibn Kathir notes that this question carries two senses, and the context supports both: is there any other god who *could* do this, and is there any other god who *deserves to be worshipped* alongside the One who does?

The idolaters did not deny that Allah creates — Ibn Kathir says they themselves admitted it, and cites their own admissions from elsewhere in the Qurʼān: *"If you ask them who created them, they will certainly say: Allah"* (31:25), and *"If you were to ask them who sends down water from the sky and gives life with it to the dead earth, they will surely say: Allah"* (29:63). Then they worshipped others alongside Him — others they themselves admitted could neither create nor provide anything. Ibn Kathir states the principle that undoes them: **the only One who deserves to be worshipped is the only One who can create and provide.**

Notice too that the closing line of each ayah shifts, tracking a diagnosis of their condition:

- 60 — *"Nay, they are a people who ascribe equals"* — Ibn Kathir: they describe others as equal and comparable to Allah.
- 61 — *"Nay, most of them do not know"* — Ibn Kathir: they do not know, in that they worship other than Allah.
- 62 — *"Little do you remember"* — Ibn Kathir: how little they think about what would guide them to the truth and show them the straight path.
- 63 — *"Exalted be Allah far above what they associate."*
- 64 — *"Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful."*

## Ayah 60: the sky, the earth, and the garden you cannot grow

**The heavens** — high and serene, with their shining stars and revolving planets. **The earth** — its varying heights and densities, and everything in it: mountains, hills, plains, rugged terrain, wildernesses, crops, trees, fruits, seas, and animals of every kind and colour and shape. **The water sent down** — sent as provision for His servants. **The gardens** that grow from it are *dhāta bahjah*: beautiful and delightful to behold. Allah does not merely feed you; He makes what feeds you a pleasure to look at.

**"It is not in your ability to cause the growth of their trees."** The One able to do that is the Creator and Provider, doing all of it alone, independent of any idol or rival. And — as the cross-references show — they knew it.

## Ayah 61: an earth that holds still

Four favours in one ayah, each read by Ibn Kathir as an act of mercy rather than a bare fact of nature.

**"He made the earth a fixed abode" (qarār)** — stable and stationary, so that it does not move or convulse; had it done so, it would be no good place for people to live. But by His grace and mercy He made it smooth and calm, unshaken. Compare 40:64: *"Allah, who made the earth a dwelling place for you and the sky a canopy."*

**"and placed rivers through its midst"** — fresh, sweet water cutting through the earth, of different types: large rivers, small ones, and some in between, caused to flow in all directions — east, west, south, north — according to the needs of people in different areas and regions. The world's rivers are a map of provision, delivered where its recipients were placed.

**"and set firm mountains upon it"** — high mountains that stabilize the earth and make it steadfast, so that it does not shake.

**"and set a barrier between the two seas"** — between the fresh water and the salt, to prevent them from mixing lest they corrupt one another. Divine wisdom, says Ibn Kathir, dictates that each should stay as it is meant to be: the sweet water is what flows in rivers among mankind, fresh and palatable so that it can water animals and plants and fruits; the salt water surrounds the continents on all sides, and is meant to be salty and undrinkable lest the air be corrupted by its smell. Compare 25:53: *"He let free the two seas, this one palatable and sweet, that one salty and bitter, and set between them a barrier and a complete partition."*

## Ayah 62: the one Allah has bound Himself to answer

**"Who responds to the distressed one (al-muḍṭarr) when he calls upon Him?"** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word. *Muḍṭarr* is derived from *iḍṭirār*, meaning to be helpless and restless under some pressing need — which happens when a person has no support and no friends. So the *muḍṭarr* is the one who has lost all hope in everyone else and turned to Allah as the sole redresser of his woes. This explanation is adopted by al-Suddī, Dhū'l-Nūn al-Miṣrī, Sahl ibn ʿAbdullāh and others, as Qurṭubī relates.

Ibn Kathir makes the same observation from experience: Allah is the One upon whom people call in times of difficulty, and the One to whom they turn when calamity strikes — *"when harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him"* (17:67); *"when harm touches you, to Him you cry aloud for help"* (16:53).

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded that a man of Balhajim asked, "O Messenger of Allah, what are you calling for?" He ﷺ said: *"I am calling people to Allah alone — the One who, if harm befalls you and you call on Him, will relieve you; and when you are lost in the wilderness and you call on Him, He brings you back; and when drought strikes and you call on Him, He makes your crops grow."* The man asked for advice, and he ﷺ said: *"Do not slander anyone, and do not think of any good deed as insignificant — even if it is only meeting your brother with a cheerful face, or emptying your vessel into the vessel of one who is asking for water. Wear your lower garment at mid-calf length, or — if you insist — let it reach your ankles, and beware of lowering the garment below the ankles, for it is a form of showing off, and Allah does not like showing off."*

The man asks the greatest question — who is worth calling on — and the advice that follows is all small kindnesses and freedom from arrogance.

**Why this particular prayer is answered.** Qurṭubī, as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, held that Allah has taken upon Himself to accept the supplication of the *muḍṭarr*, and has declared as much in this ayah. The reason he gives is that divorcing oneself from all worldly supports and connections and beseeching Allah while regarding Him as the sole redresser *is sincerity at its best*. Sincerity has a special position before Allah: whoever shows it — believer or disbeliever, pious or sinful — the divine favour turns toward him because of the blessing in sincerity itself. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to Allah's own description of the disbelievers who, when their boat is caught in a storm and they are sure of death, call on Him with total sincerity — and then, once He rescues them and brings them to land, go straight back to associating partners with Him.

The prayer the Prophet ﷺ advised for a person in this state, as Qurṭubī relates it: *"O Allah, it is Your grace I hope for; do not leave me at the mercy of myself for a moment; set right all my affairs Yourself; there is no god except You."*

**Three prayers that are answered.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a sahih (sound) hadith of the Prophet ﷺ that three supplications are surely accepted, with no room for doubt: that of an oppressed person, that of a traveller, and that of a father against his children. Qurṭubī's comment is that all three cases are the same as the supplication of a *muḍṭarr*: the oppressed person calls on Allah only after being frustrated of every worldly support and help; the traveller is away from his dear ones, and so is helpless on his journey; and a father's love and affection for his children mean he would never plead against them unless he were totally dejected and heart-broken. Al-Ājurrī, a scholar of hadith, quoted on the authority of Abū Dharr that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah has pronounced that He shall never reject an appeal from an oppressed person, even if it is made by a disbeliever.

**And if the answer does not come?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses this directly and gently. Whoever is in distress, or oppressed, or travelling, and feels his appeal has not been accepted should not be dejected or sceptical — sometimes the request is accepted but its manifestation is delayed for some wisdom Allah knows. Instead, such a person should search his soul to find out whether there was any deficiency in his sincerity or concentration while he was praying. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Kathir also relates, from al-Ḥāfiẓ Ibn ʿAsākir's biography of Fāṭimah bint al-Ḥasan Umm Aḥmad al-ʿAjaliyyah, the account of a mujāhid lured out by a treacherous companion who had pretended goodwill toward Islam until he made his move on him while they were walking along the shore. The mujāhid lifted his gaze to the sky and said: "O Allah, he has deceived me by swearing in Your name, so protect me in whatever way You will" — and he came back safe and sound. A man with nothing left but Allah, answered.

**"and makes you inheritors of the earth."** Ibn Kathir reads this as each generation inheriting from the one before it — nation after nation, generation after generation, people after people (compare 6:133, 6:165, and 2:30). He then reflects on the wisdom in it: had He willed, Allah could have created them all at one time, as He created Adam from dust; or He could have made some of them the offspring of others but caused none to die until they all died together — in which case the earth would have become constricted for them, living and earning would have become too difficult, and they would have caused inconvenience and harm to one another. But His wisdom and decree ruled that they should be created from one soul, then greatly increased in number, then made generation after generation until their time comes to an end and no one is left on earth. Then the Resurrection will come to pass, and each person will be rewarded or punished according to his deeds. Your turn on the earth is a handover, not a possession.

## Ayah 63: guidance through the dark, and wind before rain

**"Who guides you through the darknesses of the land and the sea?"** By means of what He has created of heavenly and earthly signposts — as in 16:16, *"and landmarks; and by the stars they guide themselves,"* and 6:97, *"It is He who set the stars for you, that you may guide your course by them through the darknesses of land and sea."* A traveller's whole safety rested on a star he did not place and a landmark he did not set.

**"and who sends the winds as heralds of glad tidings before His mercy?"** Ibn Kathir: ahead of the clouds which bring rain, by means of which Allah shows His mercy to servants suffering drought and despair. The wind is the announcement; the rain is the mercy. And the ayah closes not with a rebuke but with a declaration — **"Exalted be Allah above all that they associate as partners."**

## Ayah 64: from the first creation to the last, then the demand for proof

**"Who originates creation and then repeats it?"** By His might and power He begins and He repeats — as in 85:12–13, *"Verily the punishment of your Lord is severe and painful; verily He it is who begins and repeats,"* and 30:27, *"He it is who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him."* Whoever made a thing the first time is not defeated by making it again.

**"and who provides for you from the sky and the earth?"** Ibn Kathir describes the cycle: Allah sends water down from the sky as a blessing, causes it to penetrate the earth, then brings it forth as springs, and by means of it produces all kinds of crops, fruits and flowers in all their different forms and colours — *"Eat and pasture your cattle; verily, in this are signs for men of understanding"* (20:54). Compare 86:11–12 and 34:2.

Then the argument closes: **"Say: Bring forth your proofs, if you are truthful."** Ibn Kathir's remark is quiet and final — it is known that they have no proof or evidence, as in 23:117: *"Whoever invokes besides Allah any other god, of whom he has no proof, his reckoning is only with his Lord; surely the disbelievers will not be successful."*

## Living it

- **Praise, then peace, then speak.** Ayah 59 is not only theology; it is a habit. Begin your addresses — and, following the Companions, your important undertakings — with praise of Allah and ṣalāh and salām upon the Prophet ﷺ.
- **Read the world as evidence, not as scenery.** The passage is a slow walk through ordinary things — rain, a garden, a river, a mountain, a star, a wind — and asks one question of each. These are not rare wonders; they are the things you stop noticing.
- **Learn who the *muḍṭarr* is, and be honest when you are him.** The state Allah undertakes to answer is the state of having no one else. What is rewarded here is sincerity — of the kind that only arrives once everything else has been let go.
- **Do not measure Allah's response by your timetable.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's counsel stands: no dejection, no scepticism; a delayed answer may still be an answer, and the honest response is to search your own sincerity rather than to doubt Allah's promise.
- **Do not think any good deed too small.** The advice attached to the great question of ayah 62: do not slander, meet your brother with a cheerful face, pour from your vessel into another's, and keep clear of the vanity of a trailing garment.

passages.title: None knows the unseen; deniers of resurrection
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat draw a single line between what Allah alone knows and what creation can only guess at — and then show what happens to people who mistake their own ignorance for evidence. Ayat 65–66 place the knowledge of the Unseen, and above all the timing of the Resurrection, entirely with Allah, then trace the deniers' slide from not-knowing into blindness. Ayat 67–68 let those deniers speak in their own voice. Ayat 69–70 answer them — not with argument but with a command to go and look at history — and then turn to the Prophet ﷺ himself with comfort: their rejection is not his burden to carry.

## Ayat 65–66 — the Unseen belongs to Allah, and the descent of those who deny it

Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to inform all of creation that no one among the dwellers of heaven and earth knows the Unseen (*al-ghayb*) except Allah.

Notice how the announcement is framed. It does not say "people do not know"; it says **none in the heavens and the earth**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the scope: all the creatures that live in the heavens, like the angels, and all the creatures that live in this world, like humans and jinn — none of them have any knowledge of the unseen except Allah. The verse states very clearly that this is an exclusive attribute of Allah Taʿālā, which no one else shares, **not even an angel or a prophet**. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the subject is treated in detail at 6:59 in its third volume, and in a separate treatise, *Kashf al-Rayb ʿan ʿIlm al-Ghayb*, published in the author's Arabic work *Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān*, for anyone who wants to pursue it.)

Ibn Kathir focuses on the two Arabic words that carry the whole weight: **إِلَّا اللَّهُ — *illa Allāh*, "except Allah."** He calls this "an absolute exception" — an exception with nothing carved out of it and no conditions attached. The meaning is that no one knows this besides Allah; He is alone in that regard, having no partner in that knowledge. Ibn Kathir places the ayah alongside its sisters elsewhere in the Qur'an:

> "And with Him are the keys of the Unseen, none knows them but He" (6:59)

> "Verily, Allah, with Him is the knowledge of the Hour, He sends down the rain" (31:34)

and he notes that there are many other ayat which mention similar things. This is not one isolated statement to be argued over; it is a settled refrain of the Qur'an.

**The second half of ayah 65 narrows the point to one specific piece of the Unseen:** *"nor can they perceive when they shall be resurrected."* Ibn Kathir explains: the created beings who dwell in the heavens and on earth do not know when the Hour will occur. He cites Allah's words about the Hour, *"Heavy is its burden through the heavens and the earth. It shall not come upon you except all of a sudden"* (7:187) — meaning, he says, that it is a grave matter for the dwellers of heaven and earth. It will arrive without warning, on everyone at once.

Then ayah 66 comes in three strokes, each opening with **بَلْ (*bal*)** — "Nay," or "rather," the Arabic particle that sets aside what has just been said and replaces it with something further from the truth. Read them in order and you are watching a descent.

**"Nay, their knowledge …"** The first stroke turns on the word **اِدَّارَكَ (*iddāraka*)**, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid that there are different recitations of this word with correspondingly different meanings, referring readers who want the detail to the larger commentaries. Two readings are set out:

- *Completion.* On this reading the sense is: "Their knowledge and understanding will be completed in the Hereafter" — because then the truth about everything shall be laid bare. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the sting that makes this a rebuke rather than a promise: **knowledge of the truth at that time will be of no avail**, because in this world they had been contradicting the Hereafter. Certainty arrives, but it arrives too late to be worth anything.
- *Failure.* Other commentators take the word in the meaning of "having failed" and "having been lost." The sense then is that their knowledge about the Hereafter was lost, and they could not understand what it was.

Ibn Kathir gives the sense as: their knowledge and their amazement **stop short** of knowing its time. And he records that other scholars read the phrase with the meaning "their knowledge is all the same with regard to that" — that is, everyone's knowledge of the Hour is level, because nobody's reaches it.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir says that this last reading reflects the meaning of the hadith in **Sahih Muslim**, in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ replied to Jibril, when Jibril asked him when the Hour would come:

> **مَا الْمَسْؤُولُ عَنْهَا بِأَعْلَمَ مِنَ السَّائِلِ**
> "The one who is being asked about it does not know any more than the one who is asking."

Sit with that exchange. The one asked and the one asking, as Ibn Kathir puts it, were both equal in the fact that their knowledge did not extend that far. Ayah 65 stated the principle; here the Prophet ﷺ lives it out in a single sentence.

**"Nay, they are in doubt about it."** Ibn Kathir says this refers to the disbelievers in general, and reads it in the light of 18:48, where those set before their Lord in rows are told: *"Now indeed, you have come to Us as We created you the first time. Nay, but you thought that We had appointed no meeting for you (with Us)"* — meaning the disbelievers among them. The meaning here, he says, is that they doubt it will come to pass. So this stroke moves from *not knowing when* to *not being sure that*.

**"Nay, they are in complete blindness about it."** Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and final: they are blind and completely ignorant about it. Doubt at least keeps a door open; blindness does not even see the door. The three *bal*s therefore trace a slide from ignorance of the timing, to suspicion that the whole thing is untrue, to a settled inability to see it at all.

## Ayat 67–68 — the objection, in their own words

Now the Qur'an lets the deniers speak. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah tells us about the idolaters who deny the Resurrection, **considering it extremely unlikely that bodies will be re-created after they have become bones and dust**. That is the force of ayah 67: *"When we have become dust — we and our fathers — shall we really be brought forth?"* The objection is not philosophical; it is a shudder of the imagination. They look at a grave, they picture dust, and they cannot see a road back from there.

Ayah 68 adds their second argument, and Ibn Kathir paraphrases it in plain speech: *"Indeed we were promised this — we and our forefathers before"* means, "we and our forefathers have been hearing this for a long time, but in reality, we have never seen it happen." Long familiarity with a warning is being treated as evidence against it. Because nothing has arrived yet, they conclude nothing will.

From there they reach for the dismissal: **إِنْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ — "these are nothing but *asāṭīr al-awwalīn*, tales of ancients."** Ibn Kathir explains what the accusation actually claims: that the promises that bodies will be restored were taken by the people who came before us from books which were handed down from one to the other, but **they have no basis in reality**. It is the charge that revelation is inherited folklore — a story passed along so many times that its origin is a rumour. Worth noticing, as a reader: they have answered a claim about Allah's power with a claim about where old books came from.

## Ayat 69–70 — look at the land, and let go of the grief

Ibn Kathir says that, responding to their thoughts of disbelief and their belief that there would be no Resurrection, Allah told His Prophet ﷺ: *say, O Muhammad, to these people,* **"Travel in the land and see how has been the end of the criminals."**

This is a striking answer. They demanded proof of a future event; they are sent to inspect the past. Ibn Kathir identifies "the criminals" (*al-mujrimīn*) precisely: those who denied the Messengers and their message of the Resurrection and other matters. And he tells us what the traveller is meant to see: **how the punishment and vengeance of Allah struck them, and how Allah saved from among them the noble Messengers and the believers who followed them.** That double outcome — ruin for the deniers, rescue for the believers — is, in his words, an indication of the truth of the Message brought by the Messengers.

The logic is worth making explicit. The deniers said, "we have never seen it happen." The reply sends them to look at what did happen: ruined settlements they can walk through, believers delivered exactly as promised. And the verb is a command to *move* and *look* — faith invited to examine evidence, not to shut its eyes.

Then the passage turns away from the deniers entirely and speaks to the one carrying them. Ibn Kathir introduces ayah 70 with the words: **"Then, to comfort the Prophet ﷺ, Allah says …"**

*"And grieve you not over them"* — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, "do not feel sorry for them or kill yourself with regret for them." That phrase tells you what kind of man was being addressed. He was not merely exasperated by their rejection; he was grieving over it, wearing himself down over people who rejected him. Allah does not scold that tenderness — He simply lifts its weight off him.

*"Nor be straitened because of what they plot"* — to be *straitened* is to be hemmed in, squeezed, left with no room to breathe. Ibn Kathir gives the sense: do not be in distress because they plot against you and reject what you have brought, **for Allah will help and support you, and cause your religion to prevail over those who oppose you and stubbornly resist you in the east and in the west.** The remedy for a chest that has gone tight is not a change in the plotters; it is a promise about the outcome.

## Living it

**Hold the Unseen where it belongs.** Ayah 65 is a wall. Knowledge of the Unseen is, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, an exclusive attribute of Allah Taʿālā that no one else shares — not even an angel or a prophet. The believer's response to "when is the Hour?" is the Prophet's ﷺ own answer to Jibril: the one asked knows no more than the one asking.

**Do not treat delay as disproof.** The deniers' whole case in ayah 68 was that they had been hearing the warning for a long time and had never seen it happen. Every generation is tempted by that argument. Ayah 69 answers it by sending them to look at the end of people who reasoned exactly that way.

**Guard against the slide in ayah 66.** Doubt that is fed rather than examined does not stay doubt; the ayah moves from doubt to blindness. And the "completion" reading is the sober warning at the end of that road — a day when the truth about everything is laid bare, and the knowledge is of no avail to the one who finally has it.
