**Carry people, but do not carry their choices.** If the Prophet ﷺ was told not to kill himself with regret over those who refused him, then the believer who agonises over a relative who will not listen is being told something similar. Convey, care, pray — and then let the outcome rest with the One who promised His Messenger ﷺ help and support against every plot, in the east and in the west.

passages.title: Hastening the promised punishment, and Allah's knowledge
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer a taunt. The idolaters kept demanding to know the date of the Day they were being warned about — not because they wanted the answer, but because they were sure no answer would come. Ibn Kathir sums up the whole scene in a sentence: Allah is telling us how the idolaters asked about the Day of Resurrection while thinking it unlikely that it would ever come to pass.

What holds the passage together is the shape of the reply. The mockers ask a question about **time** — *when?* Allah answers first about time (ayah 72: it may be close behind you), and then moves the ground: from *when will it come* to *who is your Lord*. He is full of grace (73); He knows what their breasts conceal (74); nothing hidden in the heavens or the earth is outside a Clear Book (75). The scoffer asked for a date. What he is given is a description of the One he is mocking.

## Ayah 71: the mockery

> "And they say: 'When (will) this promise (be fulfilled), if you are truthful?'"

The translation of this ayah supplies who is being addressed: they say it **to the believers** — *all of you who keep repeating this warning, name the day.* And the reply in ayah 72 opens with **qul**, "Say", which Ibn Kathir glosses as: *'O Muhammad.'* They put the challenge to the community; Allah answers through His Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn Kathir is careful about the spirit of the question: they asked, "but thought it unlikely that it would ever come to pass." So this is not the question of a searcher. It is the noise a man makes when he has already decided the answer is nothing. That is why Allah does not respond with a date.

## Ayah 72: "perhaps" that means "close behind"

> "Say: 'Perhaps that which you wish to hasten on may be close behind you.'"

Notice what the reply refuses to do. It names no year and no hour. It says *perhaps* — and *perhaps* is far more unsettling to a man betting his life on a distant future than any date would be, because a date can be discounted until it draws near, while "perhaps, and it may already be behind you" leaves no safe stretch of time anywhere. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the same answer given in Sūrat al-Isrāʼ: *"And they say: 'When will that be?' Say: 'Perhaps it is near!'"* (17:51).

The early authorities did not read this as a bare possibility. **Ibn ʿAbbās said:** *"That which you wish to hasten on has come close to you, or some of it has come close."* Ibn Kathir reports that this was also the view of Mujāhid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʼ al-Khurāsānī, Qatādah and as-Suddī. And on the phrase *"may be close behind you"*, Ibn Kathir reports from Mujāhid: it means **it is being hastened for you**. Their own demand — *tastaʿjilūn*, "you seek to hasten" — is turned back on them. You want it rushed? It is being rushed.

Note also the precision of "**some** of what you seek to hasten." The ayah does not say *all* of it, and Ibn ʿAbbās's wording preserves that: "or some of it has come close." Part of what they were daring to arrive can reach them before the whole of it does. Ibn Kathir sets beside this the ayah: *"They ask you to hasten on the torment. And verily, Hell, of a surety, will encompass the disbelievers"* (29:54) — where the punishment they are calling for is described as encompassing them already.

So the reply to "when?" is not evasion. It is: *you are asking about the timing of something that may already be at your back.*

## Ayah 73: why it has not come yet

> "Verily, your Lord is full of grace for mankind, yet most of them do not give thanks."

Here the passage turns, and it turns towards mercy. If they are hurrying the punishment and it has not arrived, the reason is not that the warning was empty. The reason is **faḍl** — grace, bounty, favour freely given. Ibn Kathir explains the ayah as: He abundantly bestows His blessings upon them **even though they wrong themselves**, and despite that they do not give thanks for those blessings — except a few of them.

Read that against ayah 71. The very breath the mocker uses to say *"when is this promise?"* comes from the One he is mocking. The delay he treats as proof that there is nothing to fear is itself part of the grace he is failing to thank Allah for. This is the passage's deepest reversal: what looks like the absence of a response *is* a response — a reprieve. And the ayah is honest about how that reprieve is usually received: *most of them do not give thanks.* Gratitude, on this reckoning, is the rare thing, not the normal one.

Note also the address: **"your Lord"** — spoken to the Prophet ﷺ, the same one told to *"Say"* in the ayah before. Ayat 73 and 74 both open this way. The scoffers are being told a fact; the Prophet ﷺ, standing in the middle of their ridicule, is being told about *his* Lord — full of grace, and knowing exactly what is in their chests.

## Ayah 74: the answer they were not asking for

> "And verily, your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they reveal."

Now the subject shifts from the timing of the Day to the state of the questioners. What is concealed here is concealed in *their breasts* — the private interior where a person keeps what he would never say aloud. Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact and quietly devastating: **He knows what is hidden in their hearts just as He knows what is easily visible.**

That is the real reply to their question. They asked *when*, but the question was a performance. Allah's answer is: I know the sentence you spoke — and the one you did not.

Ibn Kathir gathers three ayat that state this from three different angles:

- *"It is the same (to Him) whether any of you conceals his speech or declares it openly"* (13:10) — concealing and declaring stand equal before His knowledge.
- *"He knows the secret and that which is yet more hidden"* (20:7) — beyond the secret a person is keeping there is something deeper still, and that too is known.
- *"Surely, even when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal"* (11:5).

And Ibn Kathir draws the conclusion: Allah is the Knower of the unseen in the heavens and on the earth, the Knower of **the unseen and the seen** — that which His servants cannot see, and that which they can. We affirm His knowledge as He describes it here: complete, reaching the hidden exactly as it reaches the open, and not to be measured by the knowing of creatures.

## Ayah 75: nothing left over

> "And there is nothing hidden in the heaven and the earth but it is in a Clear Book."

The passage closes by widening out from these particular hearts to everything that exists. Whatever is hidden, anywhere in the heavens or the earth, is *in a Clear Book*. Ibn Kathir pairs it with: *"Know you not that Allah knows all that is in the heaven and on the earth? Verily, it is (all) in the Book. Verily, that is easy for Allah"* (22:70) — and it is worth pausing on that last clause. What overwhelms the imagination of a creature is, for Allah, **easy**.

And so the original question is answered indirectly. They demanded to be told something hidden from them. The passage ends by saying that nothing hidden, in the heavens or the earth, is hidden from Him — it is all recorded. Their ignorance of the date was never evidence that there is nothing there. It was only evidence about them.

## Living it

**Stop treating delay as safety.** The mocker's whole argument was built on time passing without incident. Ayat 72 and 73 dismantle it from both ends: what you are waiting for may be *close behind you*, and the reason it has not arrived is a grace you have not thanked Allah for.

**Let respite make you grateful, not casual.** Ibn Kathir's note on ayah 73 — blessings poured out on people *even while they wrong themselves*, and still most do not give thanks — is not only about those idolaters. Every unpunished day is that same grace. The believing response to being given more time is to use it, and to thank Allah for it.

**Attend to the inside.** If ayah 74 is true, then the hidden self is not a private room. That should discipline us — no calculating heart behind a pious face — and it should also console us: the sincerity nobody noticed, the grief nobody heard, all of it is known to Him "just as He knows what is easily visible."

**And keep the taunt of ayah 71 in perspective.** The challenge was thrown at the believers, and the reply came through the Prophet ﷺ — beginning with "Say", and going on to speak to him of *his* Lord: full of grace, and fully aware of what those chests were concealing. When faith is ridiculed today, that is still where the answer lies.

passages.title: The Qur'an settles disputes; trust and preach on
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat move from the Qur'an's authority to the Prophet's ﷺ peace of heart. First Allah establishes what this Book is — the arbiter over disputes that the scholars of the Children of Israel could never settle among themselves (76), a guide and mercy for those who believe in it (77), with the final verdict reserved to Allah Himself (78). Then, on that foundation, comes the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ: rely on Allah, you are on plain truth (79) — and stop measuring yourself by how many respond, because the dead, the deaf and the blind were never yours to reach (80–81). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own sequence makes the link explicit: because the Qur'an is established as an authentic informant, the Prophet ﷺ is then consoled that he need not be despondent. Certainty first, calm after.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The preceding verses had used example after example of Allah's omnipotence to establish the reality of the Hereafter and the rational possibility of the dead being raised — there is no logical ambiguity in it. But a claim about the unseen is only as strong as the one who reports it: "Authenticity and establishment of any information is based on the veracity of the courier or the narrator." So Allah now identifies the informant. The reporter of this news is the Qur'an, "whose authenticity and truthfulness is beyond any doubt or contradiction."

## Ayah 76 — a Book that settles what scholars could not

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 76 as Allah telling us about His own Book: the guidance it contains, the proof it carries, and the criterion it supplies between right and wrong. And He tells us about the Children of Israel, "who were the bearers of the Tawrah and Injil."

Notice the argument Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out of this. These were not trivial disagreements; they were matters "in which the scholars of Bani Isra'il had differed strongly and could not resolve them," and the Qur'an walks in and issues the verdict they are to follow. Then comes the reasoning: "in matters where there is difference of opinion among the scholars, the only competent authority to overrule is the one who is superior in knowledge and status." A voice that can settle what the learned could not settle is, by that very fact, a voice from above them. The Qur'an's power to arbitrate is itself the evidence that it is an authentic informant — which is exactly what was needed to close the argument about resurrection.

**The word "most."** The ayah says the Qur'an narrates to them *akthar* — "most" — of that in which they differ, not every last point. Ibn Kathir's illustration shows the kind of difference that is meant.

**The test case: ʿĪsā.** Ibn Kathir gives the clearest illustration — "their different opinions about ʿĪsā. The Jews lied about him while the Christians exaggerated in praise for him, so the Qur'an came with the moderate word of truth and justice: that he was one of the servants of Allah, and one of His noble Prophets and Messengers, may the best of peace and blessings be upon him." Two errors in opposite directions — slander on one side, excess in praise on the other — and the Qur'an takes neither, but comes with the moderate word: a servant of Allah, and a noble Messenger. Ibn Kathir cites the Qur'an's own summary: *"Such is ʿĪsā, son of Maryam. (It is) a statement of truth, about which they doubt"* (19:34). Note the phrasing there — the truth is settled; the doubting is theirs.

## Ayah 77 — guide and mercy, but "for the believers"

*"And truly, it is a guide and a mercy for the believers."* Ibn Kathir: "it is guidance for the hearts of those who believe in it, and a mercy to them."

Two things are worth pausing on. First, the guidance lands **in the heart** — this is not merely information transferred; Ibn Kathir specifies it is guidance *for the hearts*. Second, the description he gives is of those "who believe in it." The same Qur'an that arbitrates in ayah 76 is named guidance and mercy in relation to the believers. That is the point ayat 80–81 will go on to explain.

## Ayah 78 — the verdict belongs to Allah

*"Verily, your Lord will decide between them by His judgement. And He is the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."*

Ibn Kathir specifies the timing: "on the Day of Resurrection." So the Qur'an gives the correct verdict now, in this life, for whoever will take it; and Allah will decide between them then.

The two names that close the ayah are not decoration; each answers a worry:

- **al-ʿAzīz**, the All-Mighty — Ibn Kathir glosses this here as might "in His vengeance." No one who rejected the truth escapes because he was powerful, well-connected, or long dead.
- **al-ʿAlīm**, the All-Knowing — "Who knows all that His servants do and say." No case is misjudged for lack of evidence; nothing said behind closed doors is missing from the file.

## Ayah 79 — "So put your trust in Allah"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this command exactly where the argument leaves off: once it is established that the Qur'an is an authentic informant, "After this the Holy Prophet ﷺ was consoled that he need not be despondent over their antagonism."

Ibn Kathir expands the command in two directions: put your trust in Allah "in all your affairs, **and convey the Message of your Lord**." Tawakkul — reliance on Allah — is not withdrawal here. It is joined in the same breath to continuing the work: you lean on Allah, and you keep conveying.

Then the reassurance: *"surely, you are on manifest truth."* Ibn Kathir: "you are following manifest truth, even though you are opposed by those who oppose you because they are doomed. The Word of your Lord has been justified against them, so that they will not believe even if all the signs are brought to them."

This is a crucial correction of instinct. Opposition feels like evidence that something is wrong with your message. Ibn Kathir reads it the other way: the truth is manifest, and the opposition is explained by the condition of those opposing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the consolation being offered: he need not be despondent over their antagonism; Allah is to make judgment in his case Himself; he should have faith in Allah, "because Allah's help and aid is with the truth. And there is no doubt that he is on the right path."

## Ayat 80–81 — why the Prophet ﷺ needed this

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the human background, and it is the most moving thing in this passage. It was the demand of the love and affection the Prophet ﷺ had for all human beings that he should save them all from the Fire by getting them to accept Allah's message. "It used to hurt him a lot if someone did not accept it. He used to feel as if someone's children were proceeding toward the fire by not heeding to the advice of his parents."

That is why, Maʿārif notes, the Qur'an has adopted different expressions to console him in many places. One such consolation came in an earlier verse of this same surah: *"And do not grieve for them, and do not be straitened because of what they plan"* (27:70). Here the consolation takes a slightly different form — an explanation. His task was only to convey the message of truth, "which he had done admirably." If someone did not accept it, that was not his fault or deficiency. Rather, it is their own fault: they are the ones who have lost their sense of direction.

**Three images for that lost direction**, as Maʿārif lays them out:

1. **The dead** — in the matter of accepting truth they were like dead bodies, and cannot take anyone's advice to their advantage.
2. **The deaf who turn their backs** — like the deaf man who does not *wish* to hear anything; rather, when someone tries to give them advice, they turn their back and go away. The ayah's own wording is exact: *"when they flee, turning their backs."*
3. **The blind** — like the blind who cannot see even if someone tries to show them the path.

Ibn Kathir makes the same identification: "you cannot cause them to hear anything that will benefit them. The same applies to those over whose hearts is a veil and in whose ears is deafness of disbelief."

## What "hearing" means here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes an important point on ayah 81. The issue is not getting sound into someone's ears: "it is not purported to make the voice reach the listener, but what is intended here is that what is conveyed should be beneficial to the addressee. The Qur'an has defined the audition as non-audition if it is not beneficial from the objective point of view."

The proof is in the ayah's own ending — *"You can make no one listen (to you) except those who believe in Our verses, then submit themselves (to Allah)"* (81). Maʿārif's reasoning: if "hearing" meant merely making them hear, the statement of the Qur'an would be contrary to facts and observation, "because there are many undeniable proofs that divine message was conveyed to the disbelievers, which they not only listened but also answered to reject." So causing to hear here means "the understanding which is beneficial."

And why call them *dead* rather than merely stubborn? Maʿārif draws out the sharp edge: even if the dead could hear and wished to accept the truth, it would not be to their avail. The dead have passed through the worldly life, "where faith and good deeds did matter." After death — both in Barzakh (the interval between death and resurrection) and in the Hereafter — all disbelievers would wish for faith and righteous deeds, "but then it would be too late." That is the force of the comparison.

Ibn Kathir describes the other side of the line, those who *do* hear: "those who have hearing and insight will respond to you, those whose hearing and sight are of benefit to their hearts and who are humble towards Allah and to the Message that comes to them through the mouths of the Messengers." And note the ayah's own order — they believe in Allah's verses, "so they submit."

## A separate question: can the dead hear?

This passage has long been cited in a discussion that Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles carefully, and it is worth reproducing its reasoning rather than only a conclusion.

**First, what the ayah does and does not say.** Maʿārif is explicit: this statement of the verse "does not bear out that the dead cannot hear. In fact this verse is silent on the subject of hearing by the dead," because its subject is beneficial understanding.

**A genuine difference among the Companions.** Maʿārif reports that this was "one of the subjects on which the exalted companions of the Holy Prophet ﷺ had different points of view." Sayyidunā ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) declared the hearing of the dead as established; Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) negated this understanding. Because of this difference, two groups formed among the Companions and the Tābiʿūn (the generation after them) — some holding that the dead do hear, others denying it. This is a real disagreement among people of knowledge, not a case of one settled view and one error.

**The precise wording of the three verses.** The subject appears in the Qur'an in three places: here in Sūrah al-Naml, in Sūrah al-Rūm with almost similar wording, and in Sūrah Fāṭir as *"You cannot cause those who are in the graves to hear."* Maʿārif points out what is worth noting in all three: not one of them declares that *the dead cannot hear*. The expression used in each is that *you cannot cause them to hear*. That consistent expression "seems to be a clear indication that the dead may have the ability to hear but we cannot cause them to listen to us."

**The verse about the martyrs.** Maʿārif sets alongside these the ayah: *"And never take those killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather they are alive, with their Lord, well-provided, happy with what Allah has given them of His grace; and they feel pleased with the good news, about those who after them could not join them, that there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve"* (3:169–170). This, he says, corroborates that even after death some intellect and perception may be left behind in the human spirit — and in the case of martyrs there is a hint that such a thing does happen. To the objection that this concerns martyrs only, his answer is that it at least establishes that such perception after death is possible; and the One who honoured the martyrs by maintaining the connection of their spirits "can also grace the other dead with the same ability."

**A narration.** Maʿārif then cites a report which he presents as a Ṣaḥīḥ hadith, giving its source as Ibn Kathir in his tafsir, from Ibn ʿUmar, with Ibn Kathir declaring it Ṣaḥīḥ: that when a person passes by the grave of a Muslim brother whom he knew when he was alive and offers salām to him, Allah returns his spirit into his body, so that he may return the salām. Maʿārif draws two conclusions from it: that the dead can hear, and that their hearing "is not in our control, but is dependent entirely on Allah's will. Whenever He wills, they can hear and whenever He does not will, they do not hear." He adds that beyond this case, "for any other situation or utterance it is not known whether the dead can hear or not."

**The balanced conclusion.** Maʿārif cites the research of Imam Ghazzālī and ʿAllāmah Subkī as reaching the same place: it is established by this Qur'anic verse and by Ṣaḥīḥ ahadith that under certain conditions the dead do hear the utterance of the living, "but it is not known whether every dead person hears the utterance at all times of all those who are living." Several possibilities remain open — that they hear at some times and not others, that they hear some people and not others, that some of the dead hear and others do not. The practical rule Maʿārif ends with is a model of scholarly restraint: "where it is established by the Sahih ahadith that the dead did hear, we should believe it; and where it is not established, both the situations are possible. Hence, we should neither accept nor deny it."

## Living it

**Convey; do not compel.** The passage draws a clean line between what is asked of you and what is not. Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 79 makes conveying the Message the Prophet's ﷺ commanded work. Ayah 81 places the outcome elsewhere: "You can only make to hear those who believe in Our Ayat." Even the Prophet ﷺ is told plainly that he cannot make the unwilling hear.

**Do not read rejection as refutation.** Ayah 79 says you are on *manifest* truth *while* being opposed. Ibn Kathir's comment is the antidote to a very modern anxiety: the opposition is explained by the state of the opponent, not by a flaw in the truth.

**Let tawakkul be fuel, not exit.** Ibn Kathir joins the two in one breath — trust Allah in all your affairs, *and convey the Message of your Lord*. Reliance on Allah is what lets you keep going when the results are not visible.

**Grieve, but within limits.** The Prophet's ﷺ pain over people who refused was real — Maʿārif describes how it used to hurt him a lot — and the Qur'an's response is consolation, not rebuke. Caring about people's fate is prophetic. Being crushed by their choices is what these ayat come to lift off the shoulders.

**Take the Qur'an as the arbiter it claims to be.** Ayah 76 presents this Book as the authority that settles what earlier scholars could not resolve. That is a claim on our own arguments too: when we differ, the honest move is to bring the matter back to it — and to aim at the same moderate word of truth and justice that Ibn Kathir describes the Qur'an bringing over ʿĪsā, refusing both the slander and the excess.

passages.title: The creature of the earth and the gathered deniers
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the closing scene of this world to the opening scene of the next. In ayah 82 the door of belief swings shut with the emergence of a strange creature from the earth that speaks to mankind; in ayat 83–85 the deniers are herded before their Lord, questioned, and struck dumb. What ties the passage together is a single phrase that opens it and closes it: **wa idhā waqaʿa al-qawlu ʿalayhim** in ayah 82 and **wa waqaʿa al-qawlu ʿalayhim** in ayah 85. Ibn Kathir renders it "And when the Word is fulfilled against them" in the first and "And the Word will be fulfilled against them" in the second; the translation given with these ayat puts it as "the decree ˹of the Hour˺ comes to pass against them" and "the decree ˹of torment˺ will be justified against them." The sentence of Allah is pronounced in this world when the time for accepting faith runs out, and it is fulfilled against them again in the next, when there is nothing left to say.

## Ayah 82: the beast of the earth

Ibn Kathir explains that this is **the beast which will emerge at the end of time, when mankind has become corrupt, has neglected the commands of Allah, and has changed the true religion.** At that point Allah will cause a beast to emerge from the earth. It was said that it will be brought from Makkah, or from somewhere else.

Two things are said about it in the ayah itself: it comes **out of the earth**, and it is brought out **to speak to them** (*tukallimuhum*).

**A creature outside the ordinary order.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the wording of the ayah itself. In its own words: "The Tannin of the word Dabbah indicates that this animal will be extra-ordinary" — the commentary reads a feature of how the word is used here in Arabic as a signal that this is no ordinary creature. It will not be born by the normal way of propagation; instead, it will emerge from the ground all of a sudden.

**What does it say?** Here the sources record two directions:

- Some commentators hold that its speech is the very message the ayah goes on to state — **"that mankind believed not with certainty in Our signs."** On this reading it communicates the message on behalf of Allah, that people did not believe in His verses; and the implication Maʿārif draws is that the time has now come when everyone would believe, but it is too late, because faith at that point would not be acceptable.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatādah** — and it was also narrated from **ʿAlī**, may Allah be pleased with him — said that it will speak words, meaning it will address them; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders this as: it will converse with people normally, as people converse among themselves.

The sources record both readings without forcing a choice between them.

## What the Sunnah says about the beast

**The ten signs.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Hudhayfah bin Asīd al-Ghifārī said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out from his room while we were discussing the matter of the Hour," and he said that the Hour will not come until they see ten signs: the rising of the sun from the west; the smoke (*ad-Dukhān*); the emergence of the beast; the emergence of Yaʼjūj and Maʼjūj; the appearance of ʿĪsā bin Maryam, upon him be peace; the Dajjāl; three land cave-ins — one in the west, one in the east and one in the Arabian Peninsula; and a Fire which will emerge from the midst of Yemen and will drive or gather the people, stopping with them wherever they stop for the night or to rest during the day. Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by **Muslim** and the **Sunan compilers** from Hudhayfah in a *mawqūf* report (one traced only to the Companion); **At-Tirmidhī** said, "It is *Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ*"; and it was also recorded by **Muslim** from Hudhayfah in a *marfūʿ* report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same hadith from the *Musnad* of Ahmad on the authority of Sayyidnā Hudhayfah, and its listing differs slightly in two items — it gives three lunar eclipses together rather than three land cave-ins, and places the fire at the Gulf of Aden, driving everyone toward the plain of gathering, stopping wherever the people stop for the night and driving them on again the next day. What both agree on is that the beast belongs to a sequence of unmistakable, public signs that precede the Hour.

**It comes near the very end.** Muslim bin al-Ḥajjāj recorded that ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr said: "I memorized a hadith from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ which I never forgot afterwards" — that the first of the signs to appear will be the rising of the sun from the west, and the emergence of the beast to mankind **in the forenoon** (*ḍuḥan*); and whichever of the two appears first, the other will follow close behind it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same conclusion plainly: the emergence of this animal would be one of the very last signs, after which the Hour will follow soon.

**Therefore: act now.** In his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, Muslim recorded from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Hasten to do good deeds before six things appear: the rising of the sun from the west; the smoke; the Dajjāl; the beast; the (death) of one of your favourite, or general affliction."* Muslim alone recorded this; Muslim also recorded a second version from Abū Hurayrah listing the same six in a different order. **Ibn Mājah** recorded a version from Anas bin Mālik, and he was the only one who recorded that version. Notice what the Prophet ﷺ does with this knowledge: he does not turn it into speculation about dates and identities. He turns it into urgency about deeds. And two of the six are not cosmic at all — a death close to you, and a general affliction — which is a way of saying that the door can close on you personally long before it closes on the world.

**The staff and the ring.** Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī recorded from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that a beast will emerge from the earth, and with it will be **the staff of Mūsā and the ring of Sulaymān**, peace be upon them both; it will strike the nose of the disbelievers with the staff and make the face of the believer bright with the ring, until when people gather to eat they will be able to recognize the believers from the disbelievers. Imam Ahmad recorded it with the two the other way round — striking with the ring and brightening with the staff — until when people gather for a meal they say to one another, "O believer," or "O disbeliever." It was also recorded by Ibn Mājah. The two emblems are worth pausing on: the staff of Mūsā and the ring of Sulaymān, the instruments of two prophets, appearing at the end of time to mark out believer from disbeliever.

**A description from Ibn az-Zubayr.** Ibn Jurayj reported that Ibn az-Zubayr described the beast — a head like a bull's, eyes like a pig's, ears like an elephant's, horns like a stag's, neck like an ostrich's, chest like a lion's, colour like a tiger's, haunches like a cat's, tail like a ram's, legs like a camel's, with a distance of twelve cubits between each pair of its joints. It brings out with it the staff of Mūsā and the ring of Sulaymān; it leaves no believer without making a white spot on his face that spreads until his whole face is shining white, and no disbeliever without a black spot that spreads until his whole face is black — so that when people trade in the marketplace they say, "How much is this, O believer?", "How much is this, O disbeliever?", and when the members of one household sit down together to eat they know who is a believer and who is a disbeliever. And the beast will say: "O so-and-so, enjoy yourself, for you are among the people of Paradise," and "O so-and-so, you are among the people of Hell." Ibn az-Zubayr then recited this very ayah as what Allah means by it.

**A necessary caution.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note of restraint that the reader should carry through this whole section: Ibn Kathir has related many things about the appearance and activities of the *Dābbah*, **most of which are not trustworthy**; therefore only that much should be trusted and believed which is contained in the Qur'an and authentic ahadith, and anything beyond that should be discarded, as it is neither of any value nor benefit. Maʿārif itself relays, via Ibn Kathir, a lengthy hadith on the authority of Sayyidnā Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUmar through Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī that this beast will emerge in Makkah from the mount of Sara and, after cleaning the dust from its head, will reach a point between the Black Stone (al-Ḥajar al-Aswad) and the Station of Ibrāhīm (Maqām Ibrāhīm) — people running helter-skelter at the sight of it, only one group of people staying behind, whose faces the beast will make glitter like stars, after which it will go out into the world and put a sign of infidelity on the face of every infidel, with no one able to get out of its grasp.

**Why the door closes.** Shaykh Jalāluddīn al-Maḥallī said — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this statement is inferred from many ahadith and the statements of the Companions, citing *Maẓharī* — that after the appearance of the *Dābbah* the obligation of inviting others to good deeds and forbidding them from evils will cease to apply, and no disbeliever will convert to Islam after that. That is the hinge of the passage: an era in which the two great works of the believer toward others come to an end. And the reason the ayah gives for sending the beast is exactly this: **"because mankind believed not with certainty in Our signs."** They would not be certain while certainty was still worth something; the beast comes because of that refusal.

## Ayat 83–84: gathered, driven, questioned

Ayah 83 shifts to the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir sets the scene: Allah tells us about the Day when the wrongdoers who disbelieved in the signs and the Messengers of Allah will be gathered before Allah, so that He will ask them about what they did in this world — **rebuking, scolding and belittling them.**

**"A *fawj* out of every nation."** Ibn Kathir explains *min kulli ummatin fawjan* as: from every people and generation, a group. No community is left out and no era is left out; the roll is called from all of them. He reads it alongside *"Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions"* (37:22) and *"And when the souls are joined with their bodies"* (81:7).

**"*Fahum yūzaʿūn*."** This is the word the passage makes you feel. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They will be pushed." ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam said: "They will be driven." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the root sense: the word is derived from *wazʿ*, which means **to stop** — the sense being that the people in front will be stopped so that those left behind can catch up; and some have taken *wazʿ* in the sense of pushing, so that they would be pushed while being brought to their stand. Either way the picture is the same: people who were free all their lives to walk away from the truth are now marshalled, with no say in where they stand or when they move.

**The question in ayah 84.** "Till, when they come" — Ibn Kathir adds: and stand before Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, in the place of reckoning — **He will say: "Did you deny My Ayat whereas you comprehended them not by knowledge, or what was it that you used to do?"** Ibn Kathir notes that this means they will be asked about **their beliefs and their deeds**. That is the shape of the question — its first half ("did you deny My signs") concerns creed, its second half ("or what was it that you used to do") concerns action. And it is a question that indicts by being asked, matching what Allah says elsewhere of such a person: *"He neither believed nor performed Salah! But on the contrary, he denied and turned away"* (75:31–32).

**"Whereas you comprehended them not by knowledge."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this phrase carefully. There is an allusion here that falsifying the message of Allah is by itself a great sin — but especially when one falsifies it **without giving it any consideration or thought**, then the crime is doubled. This has brought to light that if an issue is duly considered and thought over and the person still could not get to the truth, in that situation the intensity of the crime is reduced. But Maʿārif is explicit that this concession has a limit: denial of the existence of Allah and of His Oneness would not save anyone from infidelity and from adopting the wrong path, and would lead to perpetual torment, because these are such self-evident matters that any mistake of judgement is not allowed in them. The point is sobering in a very ordinary way: rejection of revelation passed without a hearing is precisely what Allah's question exposes.

## Ayah 85: the sentence, and the silence

"And the Word will be fulfilled against them, because they have done wrong, and they will be unable to speak." Ibn Kathir: the proof will be established against them and they will have no excuse whatsoever — as Allah says, *"That will be a Day when they shall not speak. And they will not be permitted to put forth any excuse"* (77:35–36). **They will be stunned and speechless, unable to give any answer.** And Ibn Kathir gives the reason: this is because they wronged themselves in the world, and now they have returned to the One Who sees the unseen and the seen, from Whom nothing can be hidden.

Feel the symmetry with ayah 82. There, a beast is brought out with the power of speech precisely because mankind believed not with certainty — *tukallimuhum*, "to speak to them." Here, human beings are unable to speak — *lā yanṭiqūn*. Speech is handed to a creature that was never asked to argue, and taken from those who argued all their lives. And the same phrase, *waqaʿa al-qawlu ʿalayhim*, frames both ends: the Word fulfilled against them at the end of the world is the Word fulfilled against them at the reckoning.

## Living it

**1. Believe now, while believing still costs something.** The reason ayah 82 gives for the whole event is that mankind "believed not with certainty in Our signs." Certainty will reach everyone eventually — at the sight of the beast, at the standing before Allah. What is asked of you is certainty *before* the evidence becomes irresistible; and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān warns that when that time comes, faith would not be acceptable then.

**2. Take the Prophet's ﷺ own conclusion from these signs.** He did not respond to them with prediction; he responded with *"Hasten to do good deeds"* — and among the six he named a death close to you and a general affliction. Whatever good you are postponing until you are older, freer, more settled: that is the deed this hadith is about.

**3. Do not reject what you have never examined.** Ayah 84 does not only condemn denial; it condemns denial *"whereas you comprehended them not by knowledge."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the mirror-point unavoidable: falsifying the message of Allah without giving it any consideration or thought doubles the crime. An opinion about revelation that you have never actually thought through is not a neutral thing — and ayah 84 shows it being asked about, out loud, before the One from Whom nothing can be hidden.

And notice where the passage leaves the deniers: gathered, driven, questioned, and silent. Ibn Kathir's summary of why is the whole lesson in one line — they wronged themselves in the world, and now they have returned to the One Who sees the unseen and the seen, from Whom nothing can be hidden. The tongue that had every argument in this life has nothing to say in that place. Better to use it now, while it is still ours to use.

passages.title: Night, day, the Trumpet, and the final reckoning
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the argument of Sūrah al-Naml by setting two scenes side by side: the quiet, unremarkable turning of night into day, and the Day when a horn is blown and the mountains themselves come loose. What binds them is one claim — the Power that arranges your sleep and your working hours is the same Power that will end the world and question you about it.

## The silence that comes just before

The passage does not begin cold. In ayat 83–85 Allah describes gathering from every nation and generation a group (*fawj*) of those who denied His signs, "and they shall be driven." Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, explained the word as "they will be pushed"; ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said, "they will be driven." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the verb comes from *wazʿ*, whose root sense is **to stop** — the ones in front are stopped so that those left behind can catch up; others took the word in the sense of *pushing*, so that they would be pushed as they are brought to their stand.

Then comes the question in ayah 84: "Did you deny My signs when you had not comprehended them in knowledge — or what was it that you used to do?" Ibn Kathir notes they are asked about both their beliefs and their deeds. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: to reject Allah's message is itself a grave sin, but to reject it *without ever having considered it* doubles the crime. If a person genuinely weighed a matter and still failed to reach the truth, the intensity of the offence is lessened — yet this concession never extends to denying Allah's existence and His Oneness, because these are self-evident matters, and no mistake of judgement is allowed in them.

And in ayah 85 the word falls upon them "and they will not speak." Ibn Kathir: they will be stunned and speechless, unable to give any answer, because they wronged themselves in the world and have now returned to the One who sees the unseen and the seen, from whom nothing can be hidden.

Hold on to that silence. It is the hinge. Ibn Kathir says that Allah now "points out His complete power, immense authority and greatness, all dictating that He is to be obeyed and that His commands must be followed, and that the message of inescapable truth brought by His Prophets must be believed in." That is what ayah 86 is doing.

## Ayah 86 — the evidence He chose to produce

Of all the proofs available, the one He produces is the most ordinary thing in a human life: **night and day**.

"We made the night for them to rest in." Ibn Kathir explains that because of the darkness of the night people halt their activities and calm themselves down, recovering from the exhausting efforts of the day. "And the day sight-giving" — meaning filled with light, so that they can work and earn a living, travel, engage in business, and do the other things they need to do.

And the ayah closes: "in this are signs for a people who believe." The evidence is public and free; every human being on earth receives it. But it registers as a *sign* only in a heart willing to read it. The deniers of ayah 85 had these two signs delivered to them every day of their lives.

## Ayah 87 — the Trumpet

**What the Ṣūr is.** Ibn Kathir reports that the Ṣūr is described in the hadith as "a horn which is blown into," and that, according to the hadith about the Ṣūr, it is the angel Israfil who blows into it by the command of Allah. He will blow into it the first time, and blow it for a long time; this signals the end of the life of this world, and the Hour comes upon the most evil of people ever to live.

**Why the word is *fazi'a* and not something else.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up: *fazaʿ* means being nervous or perplexed. Another ayah on the same subject (39:68) uses *ṣaʿiqa* instead — losing consciousness. If both ayat are taken to refer to the *same* blowing, the sum of the two words is a sequence within one event: everyone first becomes nervous and perplexed, then loses consciousness, and ultimately dies.

**How many blasts?** Here the scholars genuinely differ, and the sources report the difference rather than settling it:

- Ibn Kathir's account describes **three** stages: the blast of the Ṣūr that terrifies everyone, then the blast that causes them to die, then the blast that resurrects them to meet the Lord of the worlds.
- Qatadah and some other imams of tafsir took this ayah to refer to the **second** blowing, when the dead are resurrected — so the meaning would be that all the dead will get up perplexed.
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the three-blowing view (a blowing of *fazaʿ*, a blowing of *ṣaʿq*, and the blowing for resurrection), but notes, citing Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, that **only two blowings are mentioned in the Qur'an and the Sahih ahadith**.

Between the two blowings there is a gap: Ibn Mubarak has quoted Hasan al-Basri that the Prophet ﷺ said there will be a forty-year gap between them (cited via Qurtubi in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān).

**"Except whom Allah wills."** Ibn Kathir identifies these as **the martyrs**, "for they are alive, with their Lord, and being provided for." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān holds that the exception here is from *fazaʿ* — there will be people who will not be nervous at all — and reports a hadith from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that these people are the martyrs (a Sahih hadith according to Ibn al-ʿArabi, via Qurtubi). Saʿid ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, likewise said the exception applies to the martyrs, who will assemble around the ʿArsh wearing their swords. Qushayri observed that the prophets are the very first included among them, because they hold the status of martyrs as well, and their position as prophets is higher still.

There is a second view attached to the parallel ayah in Sūrah az-Zumar (39:68), where the exception is understood — according to one hadith — to mean six angels: Jibra'il, Mika'il, Israfil, the Angel of Death, and the bearers of the ʿArsh, who will not die at that blowing, though the same hadith explains that they too will die later. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the pattern: those who hold that *fazaʿ* and *ṣaʿq* belong to the same blowing take the exception here also to be those angels; those who hold that they belong to two different blowings take the exception here to be the martyrs.

**"And all shall come to Him, humbled."** *Dākhirīn* — Ibn Kathir explains it as humbling themselves and obeying Him, with no one going against His command. He connects it to "the Day when He will call you, and you will answer with His praise and obedience" (17:52) and "then afterwards when He will call you by a single call, behold, you will come out from the earth" (30:25).

## What the Sunnah adds

Imam Muslim bin Al-Hajjaj recorded from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that the Dajjal will emerge in his Ummah and remain for forty — the narrator was unsure whether he said forty days, forty months, or forty years — then Allah will send ʿIsa son of Maryam, who looks like ʿUrwah bin Masʿud, and he will search for him and destroy him. Then mankind will remain for seven years during which there will not be any enmity between any two people. Then Allah will send a cool wind from the direction of Syria, and no one will be left on the face of the earth who has even a speck of goodness or faith in his heart, but it will take him — "even if he entered into the heart of a mountain, the wind would follow him and seize him."

The hadith continues: the most evil of people will remain, "as nimble as birds," more temperamental than wild beasts, recognising nothing good and denouncing nothing evil. The Shaytan will appear to them and command them to worship idols — and in spite of this their provision will be plentiful and they will lead comfortable lives. Then the Ṣūr will be blown, "and no one will hear it but he will tilt his head to hear the sound." Ibn Kathir explains this as tilting the head so that they can better hear the sound coming from the heavens. The first person to hear it will be a man setting up the tank for watering his camels; he will fall down, and all the other people will fall down. Then Allah will send rain like dew, from which the bodies of the people will grow. The Trumpet is blown again, and they get up and look around. Then it is said: "O mankind! Go to your Lord!" — "and they will be stopped, for they are to be questioned." Then: "Bring forth the people who are to be sent to the Fire." "How many are they?" "Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine." That, the hadith says, is the Day which will make the children grey-headed.

Notice the wording there — "they will be stopped, for they are to be questioned" — beside the *wazʿ* of ayah 83, whose root sense is *to stop*, and the questioning of ayah 84.

Ibn Kathir also relates, from the hadith about the Ṣūr, that when it is blown for the third time Allah will command the souls to be put into the hole of the Ṣūr; then Israfil blows into it, after the bodies have grown in their graves and resting places, and the souls fly out — the believers' souls glowing with light, the disbelievers' souls looking like darkness — and Allah says: "By My might and majesty, every soul will go back to its body." The souls come back to their bodies and go through them like poison going through a person who has been bitten or stung, and the people get up, brushing off the dirt of their graves. As Allah says, "the Day when they will come out of the graves quickly as racing to a goal" (70:43).

## Ayah 88 — the mountains you thought were solid

**A verb with two tenses.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that *tarā* is used in Arabic for both the present and the future tense, so this ayah carries two sound readings:

1. *"You will see"* — the scene on that Day itself: the mountains, uprooted and blown like clouds, will appear stationary to the onlookers while in reality moving swiftly. Most of the commentators have interpreted the ayah this way.
2. *"You see"* — the present state of the mountains: you look at them now, they look stationary, and an ordinary onlooker thinks they will remain fixed forever and never move from their place — yet on that Day they will be floating like clouds. This is the reading Maulana Ashraf Thanawi adopted, and the translation above follows it.

**Why the illusion is real.** The commentary gives the reason: when huge bodies whose beginning and end are not visible to the eye move in any direction, one does not perceive their movement, no matter how swiftly they move — they look like stationary objects although they are moving. You can experience this looking at a mass of cloud hanging overhead; you discover its movement only when it has moved so far that a part of the sky is left bare towards the horizon.

**The stages of the mountains.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi and Ruh ul-Maʿani) gathers what the Qur'an says about the mountains on that Day into five conditions:

1. Crushing and earthquake, enveloping all the mountains of the world — "when the earth is ground to powder" (89:21), "when the earth is shaken with a mighty shaking" (99:1).
2. Their big rocks become like carded wool (101:5), at the time when the sky becomes like molten copper (70:8–9).
3. The carded wool no longer remains a homogeneous body but turns into very fine particles — "and the mountains crumbled and became a dust scattered" (56:5–6).
4. Those fine particles are dispersed — "My Lord will blow them up totally" (20:105).
5. The fine particles engulf the land like a cloud of dust and are driven up by the winds — appearing stationary although moving swiftly, which is our ayah, 27:88.

Some of these conditions take place at the first blowing of the Ṣūr and some after the second, when the world is made an absolutely flat plain — "a level smooth plain, in which you see nothing crooked or curved" (20:105–107) — with no cave or mountain left, nor any building or tree. Ibn Kathir gathers the same picture from 52:9–10, 20:105–107 and 18:47.

**"The work of Allah, who perfected everything."** *Ṣunʿ* means a skilful act; *itqān* means to make a thing perfect and firm. Ibn Kathir: He does this by His great power; He has perfected all that He has created and fashioned it according to His wisdom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the phrase as related to all the preceding subjects — the alternation of day and night, the blowing of the Ṣūr, the resulting conditions of that Day — emphasising that none of this should amaze or astonish anyone, because the Creator behind it is not a man or an angel of limited knowledge and power, but the Lord of all the worlds. Read more narrowly, as referring only to the sentence just before it, it means that the mountains looking stationary while in reality moving is nothing astonishing, since none of this is beyond the power of Allah, who is All-Powerful.

**"He is well-acquainted with what you do."** In a single breath the ayah drops from cosmic demolition to your private conduct. Ibn Kathir: He knows all that His servants do, good or evil, and He will reward or punish them accordingly. The same precision that shaped the mountains is trained on your record.

## Ayat 89–90 — two ways of arriving

The Arabic in both ayat is *man jā'a bi* — "whoever **comes with**." You do not merely arrive on that Day; you arrive **carrying something**.

**What counts as the *ḥasanah*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the reported meanings: Ibrahim explained it as the *kalimah*, "there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah"; Qatadah — quoted by Ibn Kathir too — explained it as what is "sincerely for Allah alone"; some took it to include complete submission. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the necessary condition: a person's righteous acts can be considered righteous only when he fulfils the first condition of having faith in Allah.

**"Better than it."** Ibn Kathir notes that Allah has explained elsewhere in the Qur'an that He will give ten like it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, records the view that "better" here means the reward of one good deed will be awarded from ten times up to seven hundred times more. And it is more than arithmetic: it means being graced with the eternal bounties of Paradise, and escaping all troubles and torments for good.

**"And they will be safe from the terror of that Day."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *fazaʿ* here as any big calamity or perplexity, and then draws out the most searching lesson in the passage. While living in this world, every pious person is scared of his fate in the Hereafter — and as a matter of fact he *should* be, in the light of the ayah "the torment of their Lord is not something to be secure from" (70:28). It is for this reason that even the prophets, the Companions and the righteous were always frightened and daunted. But after the account-taking, those who bring the *ḥasanah* with them will be free from all fear and grief and will live forever in complete tranquillity. Fear now buys security then. Ibn Kathir sets the same promise beside "the greatest terror will not grieve them" (21:103), "is he who is cast into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?" (41:40), and "they will reside in the high dwellings in peace and security" (34:37).

**Ayah 90 — the other arrival.** "Whoever comes with an evil deed — they will be cast down on their faces in the Fire." Ibn Kathir explains this of whoever comes to Allah with evil deeds and with no good deeds to his credit, or whose evil deeds outweigh his good deeds. The face — the part a person spends a lifetime protecting and presenting — goes first.

Then the closing sentence of the whole passage: "Are you being recompensed anything except what you used to do?" Nothing is added to their account. It is their own record read back to them. Look at the asymmetry the two ayat set up: the good deed is repaid with something *better* than itself, multiplied many times over; the evil deed is repaid with *exactly* what was done, nothing more. Pure generosity on one side, pure justice on the other.

## Living it

The passage asks three concrete things.

**Read the ordinary as a sign.** Ayah 86 does not send you to a miracle. Tonight you will lie down and the darkness will do to you what Ibn Kathir described — halt your activity, calm you, let you recover from the day's exhausting efforts. Tomorrow the light will be handed back so you can work and earn. Ibn Kathir shows Allah producing exactly this as the proof of His power right after the deniers fall silent; taking it as *āyāt* rather than as weather is what the closing words of the ayah ask of "a people who believe."

**Come carrying something, and make sure it is sincere.** Qatadah's gloss is not decorative: what qualifies as a *ḥasanah* is what is done for Allah alone, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it rests on faith in Allah first. That is a question about motive, asked now, while it can still be answered differently.

**Let fear do its work here so that it does not have to do it there.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point about the prophets, the Companions and the righteous living in dread is not gloom; it is the very thing that stands behind "they will be safe from the terror on that Day." Security on the Day belongs to those who did not feel too secure before it.

passages.title: The Prophet's commission and closing praise
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat close Surah an-Naml. After all the surah has recounted, Allah turns and tells His Messenger ﷺ to state plainly, in his own voice, what he has been put here to do — and then to end not with argument but with praise.

What binds the passage together is a single frame: **"I have been commanded only…"** Everything the Prophet ﷺ says here he says as a man under orders. Four instructions run through the three ayat — worship your Lord, be of the Muslims, recite the Qur'an to people, and say *al-hamdu lillah* — and the passage ends by handing the outcome back to the One who gave the orders: "And your Lord is not unaware of what you do."

## "I have been commanded only" — a messenger, not an inventor

Ibn Kathir opens simply: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to say, *"I have been commanded only to worship the Lord of this city, Who has sanctified it and to Whom belongs everything."*

He reads it alongside another verse where the Prophet ﷺ is told to say: "O you mankind! If you are in doubt as to my religion, then I will never worship those whom you worship besides Allah. But I worship Allah Who causes you to die" (10:104). The tone in both places is the same — a line drawn, calmly, in public. He is not negotiating a settlement between his religion and theirs. He is reporting his instructions.

That framing matters for how the whole passage lands. Everything difficult in it — the rejection, the people who go astray, the waiting for signs — sits inside the security of a man who knows exactly what he was told to do.

## "the Lord of this city" — Makkah named with honour

Allah is the Lord of everything; so why is He named here as **"the Lord of this city"**?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the majority of the commentators take *al-baldah* ("the city") to mean Makkah. Allah is the Lord of all the worlds and the Lord of the heavens and the earth — and precisely for that reason, singling Makkah out in this way is meaningful: it is done to show the city's revered splendour, and its respect and honour in the sight of Allah.

Ibn Kathir makes a related observation. The fact that the word *Rabb* (Lord) is connected to the word "city" — "the Lord of this city" — is itself a sign of honour and of divine care for that city. He compares it with the verse about the Sacred House: "So let them worship the Lord of this House, Who has fed them against hunger, and has made them safe from fear" (106:3–4). The pattern is the same in both places: the Lord identifies Himself by His care for a place and for the people in it.

## "Who has sanctified it" — the meaning of *ḥaram*

**"…Who has sanctified it"** (*alladhī ḥarramahā*). Ibn Kathir explains this as: the One Who made it a sanctuary by His Law and by His decree, making it sanctified.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. *Ḥaram* comes from *taḥrīm*, which means "to prohibit" and also means "complete respect and veneration"; and because of that respect and veneration, the special religious prohibitions that apply to Makkah and the land around it are included in the word. So, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lists:

- Whoever takes refuge in the Ḥaram is secure.
- It is not allowed to kill anyone in the Ḥaram, or to take revenge there.
- Even hunting animals and cutting trees is not permitted within the precincts of the Ḥaram.

These restrictions are enjoined in the verse "and whoever enters there is secure" (3:97); some of them appear at the beginning of Surah al-Māʼidah; and the verse "do not kill game when you are in iḥrām" (5:95) — *iḥrām* being the consecrated state a pilgrim enters — also belongs to this subject.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that it was reported in the Two Sahihs that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "On the day of the conquest of Makkah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Verily, this city was made sacred by Allah the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred by the sanctity of Allah until the Day of Resurrection. Its thorny bushes should not be cut, its game should not be chased, and its lost property should not be picked up except by one who would announce it publicly and none is allowed to uproot its thorny shrubs…'" Ibn Kathir adds that this was reported in Sahih, Hasan and Musnad narrations, through various routes, by such a large group that it is absolutely unquestionable, as he explained in the appropriate place in the book Al-Ahkam.

Sit with what is being said there. The city's sanctity is not something anyone confers or suspends: Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, and it remains sacred by *Allah's* sanctity until the Day of Resurrection. Even the smallest details follow from that — a thorn bush, a startled animal, a lost item on the ground. The reverence is not sentimental; it reaches all the way down into how a person walks through the place.

## "and to Whom belongs everything"

Ibn Kathir flags the move exactly: this is **a statement of general application following a specific statement**. He is the Lord of this city — and He is the Lord and Sovereign of all things, and there is no god worthy of worship besides Him.

That order is worth pausing on. It begins where the audience already feels reverence — the city — and then widens the frame until nothing is left outside His ownership. A person can be attached to a holy place and still misunderstand its Lord. Ayah 91 does not let the attachment stop at the stones.

## "and I am commanded to be from among the Muslims"

Ibn Kathir gives a working definition of *muslimīn* here in three strands: those who believe in Allah alone, who are sincere towards Him, and who obediently follow His commands. Belief, sincerity of heart, obedience of the limbs.

And note the wording Ibn Kathir gives: not "to be the leader of the Muslims" but "to be *from among* the Muslims." The one who delivers the command is himself under it.

## "And that I should recite the Qur'an" (ayah 92)

Recitation here is not private devotion. Ibn Kathir explains it as: to people, so as to convey it to them. He cites "This is what We recite to you of the Ayat and the Wise Reminder" (3:58) and "We recite to you some of the news of Musa and Firʿawn in truth" (28:3), and sums up the Prophet's ﷺ own sense of his role in five words: **"I am a conveyer and a warner."**

So the Qur'an moves in a chain — recited to him, recited by him to the people. His task is transmission, faithfully and audibly.

## The results are not his to carry

"Then whosoever receives guidance, receives it for the good of himself; and whosoever goes astray, say: 'I am only one of the warners.'"

This is the emotional heart of ayah 92. Guidance, when it happens, is a good the person receives for himself. And when someone turns away, the Prophet ﷺ is given a sentence to say rather than a burden to shoulder.

Ibn Kathir unpacks that sentence beautifully. The meaning is: *I have an example to follow in the Messengers who warned their people, and did what they had to do in order to convey the Message to them and fulfil the covenant they had made.* Allah will judge the nations they were sent to. Ibn Kathir supports this with two verses:

- "Your duty is only to convey and on Us is the reckoning" (13:40).
- "But you are only a warner. And Allah is a Protector over all things" (11:12).

Read the phrase again: "I am only one **of the warners**" — he is placed in a line of Messengers who did exactly this work before him. The rejection he is meeting is not a sign that something has gone wrong with his mission; it is the ordinary weather every warner before him stood in.

**Living it.** Anyone who calls others to Allah — a parent, a teacher, a friend who shared a verse and watched it ignored — is given their job description here. You are responsible for the conveying: clear, honest, sustained. You are not responsible for the outcome, and grieving as though you were is taking on work Allah did not assign you.

## "And say: all praise and thanks be to Allah" (ayah 93)

The surah could have ended on the note of people going astray. Instead the last instruction is *praise*.

Ibn Kathir explains what the praise is *for*: praise be to Allah, Who does not punish anyone except after establishing the plea against him and warning him, leaving him with no excuse. That is, the *al-hamdu lillah* of ayah 93 is praise for the perfection of Allah's justice. No one will be seized having never been told. Every warner sent, every recitation delivered — all of it is Allah leaving no one with an excuse before He judges. A believer who understands that says *al-hamdu lillah* not despite the warning but because of it.

## "He will show you His signs, and you shall recognize them"

The response to the deniers is not a fresh argument but a promise. Ibn Kathir sets it beside another verse: "We will show them Our signs in the universe, and in themselves, until it becomes manifest to them that this is the truth" (41:53). Signs in the wide world, and signs in the person's own self — and the outcome named there is that the truth becomes clear to them.

## "And your Lord is not unaware of what you do"

The final clause of the surah. Ibn Kathir's gloss is stark and simple: on the contrary, **He witnesses and sees all things.**

Ibn Kathir then closes the surah by mentioning two lines of verse that Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy upon him, used to recite — Ibn Kathir notes that it is not settled whether Imam Ahmad wrote them himself or someone else did:

> "If you are alone one day, do not say, 'I am alone.' Rather say, 'Someone is watching me.' Do not think that Allah will let His attention wander for even an instant, or that anything is hidden from Him."

That is the passage's last word turned into a habit. Ayah 93 does not say this as a piece of information; it says it as a companion for your private hours. The one who lives with it is never truly unobserved — and therefore never truly alone.

## Holding the three together

Put the commands side by side and a whole life of faith appears in miniature:

- **Worship** (ayah 91) — your relationship with Allah, anchored in His ownership and sovereignty over all things.
- **Submit** (ayah 91) — belief in Allah alone, sincerity towards Him, obedient following of His commands.
- **Recite and convey** (ayah 92) — your duty to others, with the reckoning left to Allah.
- **Praise** (ayah 93) — the settled posture of the heart, before signs that are still to come and a Lord who is not unaware of anything.

**A closing footnote.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends its commentary on Surah an-Naml with a dated personal note: *al-ḥamdu lillāh* — "Today on Shawwal 24, 1391 Hijrah the commentary of Surah An-Naml is complete." The author records that war had broken out, that aeroplanes were pounding Karachi heavily, that bombs were being dropped every night on the civil population as well, that the nights were under complete blackout and the houses were jolted by the explosions — and that by the grace of Allah there was no break in the writing of this commentary: during the last ten days of the war, twenty pages were written. He opens that note with the very word ayah 93 commands: *al-ḥamdu lillāh*. It is hard to imagine a more fitting illustration of what this passage asks of a believer.
